PAGES.TITLE: Software and Licenses
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Which libraries Galaxie Blog uses, what each one is for, and the license terms, including the ones that limit commercial use.
PAGES.BODY:
Portions of Galaxie Blog are built from other people's software. Most of it is free to use, including commercially. A few parts are not, and you should know which ones before you build a business on the blog. This page lists the main libraries, what each one is for, and the license terms that apply.

Table of Contents

What Licenses Mean for Your Site

A license is a promise from the author about what you may do with their code. Some licenses allow almost anything, some require you to share changes, and some allow personal or non-profit use only. The feature pages in these docs name the library behind each feature, and link here, so you can check the terms for the parts you use.

This page is a summary, not legal advice. The license text that ships with each library is the authority. If you plan to sell a site built on Galaxie Blog, read the licenses yourself or ask a lawyer.

Who Maintains the Software

The Galaxie Blog developers maintain every library listed on this page. Blog owners do not need to install, update, or patch them. Library updates arrive with regular Galaxie Blog releases, and the upgrade process brings them in. There are no plugins to find, buy, or keep current, so a Galaxie Blog site does not depend on a separate set of third-party add-ons to stay working.

The one step owners take is upgrading. Upload the new release files to your server, then open Blog Updates in the admin site and click Update Galaxie Blog's database. The full steps are in Updating Galaxie Blog.

The licenses are listed here so you know the terms. They are not a list of tasks for you.

Summary Table

  • Kendo UI Core (widgets, grids, windows). Free and open source. You may use and distribute it commercially. The commercial Kendo UI product is a separate purchase, and this blog does not use it.
  • GLightbox 3.3.1 (the enlarged view for galleries and images). Licensed under the MIT license, which allows commercial use with the copyright notice kept.
  • TinyMCE 5.5.1 (the post editor). Licensed under the GNU Lesser General Public License 2.1. Commercial use is allowed. Changes to the TinyMCE files must be shared under the same license, and the blog's own changes are listed in its patch notes.
  • GreenSock (TweenMax, ScrollToPlugin) (animation). Released under GreenSock's standard "no charge" license, which allows commercial use. Some GreenSock plugins are sold under a separate Club license. The blog uses only the standard plugins.
  • Swiper (carousels), Plyr (video player), three.js and Vanta (animated backgrounds), Uppy (uploads), Day.js (dates), Grapick and Pickr (gradient and color pickers), jsGrid, ScrollMagic, Prism (code highlighting), CodeMirror 5, and get-video-id. These are released under the MIT license, which allows commercial use with the copyright notice kept.
  • p5.js. Licensed under the GNU Lesser General Public License 2.1.
  • Azure Maps (maps and routes). A paid Microsoft service, not an open-source library. You supply your own key, and Microsoft's terms apply to your usage.

Licenses Worth Knowing About

Earlier FancyBox Use

Earlier releases of Galaxie Blog used FancyBox 2 for the enlarged view in galleries. FancyBox 2 is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 3.0, so it is free for personal and non-profit sites. A commercial site needs the author's permission, which the author sells as a paid license. This version no longer includes FancyBox, so new installs are not affected.

TinyMCE and Sharing Changes

TinyMCE is licensed under the LGPL, which is business-friendly. The rule that matters is that changes to TinyMCE's own files must be shared under the same license. Galaxie Blog's changes to TinyMCE, such as support for WebP images, are documented in its patch notes, and the blog's source code is public.

What You Are Responsible For

  • Azure Maps costs. Your key is billed to your Azure account.
  • Keep copyright notices. MIT and LGPL licenses both require the notice to stay in the code.
  • Check before you sell. A non-commercial license changes what you can charge for.

Gotchas

  • The commercial Kendo product is not used here. The Kendo UI Core files are the open-source ones.
  • Earlier releases used FancyBox. It limits commercial use, so check it on any site that runs an earlier release commercially.
  • This page is not legal advice. Read the license text that ships with each library.

PAGES.TITLE: Credits
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Where Galaxie Blog came from, the people who helped shape it, and the open-source projects and hosts it relies on.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog stands on other people's work: the blog it grew out of, the people who helped shape it, the open-source libraries it is built with, and the hosts that run its sites. This page says thank you, and points to where each piece came from.

Table of Contents

  • Where Galaxie Blog Came From
  • Charlie Arehart
  • Open-Source Libraries
  • Hosting
  • Images and Photography
  • Your Contributions

Where Galaxie Blog Came From

Galaxie Blog began as a revival of BlogCFC, the open-source ColdFusion blog that Raymond Camden first released in 2005. BlogCFC powered a great many ColdFusion blogs, and bringing it back to life was the original inspiration for this project. Portions of Galaxie Blog's server-side code still come from BlogCFC, and core files such as the main blog component and the RSS feed still credit Raymond in their headers.

Since then, Galaxie Blog has had four major releases, starting in 2018. It now supports both Lucee and Adobe ColdFusion, uses Hibernate ORM for its database work, and has grown its own editor, themes, page collections, and media features. Its roots are still BlogCFC, and that debt is gladly acknowledged.

Charlie Arehart

Thank you to Charlie Arehart, who is, as always, a trusted person to bounce ideas off of and ask for advice and gave Galaxie Blog its name.

Open-Source Libraries

Much of what you see in the browser - the editor, the grids and windows, the galleries, carousels, video player, maps, and animated backgrounds - is built with open-source libraries. Thank you to every author and contributor behind them. Each one, what it is used for, and its license terms are listed in Software and Licenses.

Hosting

  • Media3 provides the Adobe ColdFusion Windows hosting for gregoryalexander.com, where Galaxie Blog is developed and used every day, and for CFBlogs.org, the ColdFusion community's blog aggregator.
  • Viviotech provides the Lucee Linux hosting for galaxieblog.org.

Running the blog on both engines, with real traffic, is how many of its bugs are found and fixed before a release.

Images and Photography

Gregory Alexander either owns the copyright to, or has the rights to use, the images and photographs on this site. If an image is not part of the Galaxie Blog distribution, and instead belongs to a post or a comment, please contact the author of that post or comment before using it.

Your Contributions

Galaxie Blog is free and open source, and it gets better when people share. If you have an idea, a fix, or a theme you built, you are welcome to contribute it. Comments, bug reports, and suggestions all help.

PAGES.TITLE: Members: Everyone in One List
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Everyone who books, signs up, subscribes or sends a form, in one list: member accounts, pictures, profiles on the site, privacy requests and the Member Log.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog has two kinds of people. Users run the blog and sign in to the admin site. Members are everyone else: people who booked, signed up for an event, subscribed, sent a form, or made an account. Members keeps all of them in one list, so each person shows once, with everything they've done.

Table of Contents

  • The Members List
  • A Person's Page
  • Member Accounts and Signing In
  • Pictures
  • Shown on the Site
  • Deleting Someone, and Their Data
  • The Member Log
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

The Members List

Click Members on the admin home page. Everyone is listed once, matched by email address, with what they've done: Member, On the site, Subscriber, Booked, Signed up, Forms, and "Also a user" when the address belongs to one of your users. Commenters aren't included; they have their own moderation screen.

  • The buttons at the top filter the list, with how many people each holds: All, Members, On the site, Subscribers, Bookings, Event sign-ups and Forms.
  • With more than 10 people, the list becomes a grid you can sort, search and page through.
  • Click a name or Open for the person's page. Click an email address to write to them.
  • Add person adds someone to show on the site who hasn't booked or signed up, for example a presenter who hosts an event.

A Person's Page

A person's page shows their details, what they've done, and whether they're shown on the site, then their bookings (each opens the booking), their event sign-ups and forms, and their email subscriptions. For someone with an account it also shows when they joined, when they were last seen, how many devices they stay signed in on, and the Block and Sign-ins buttons.

Member Accounts and Signing In

With member accounts on, visitors can sign in to see their bookings and sign-ups in one place, and have their name, email and phone filled in for them on forms and bookings. There are no passwords: a visitor enters their email address and clicks the one-time link the blog emails them. Members never have access to the admin site.

  • Turn them on in Blog Options > Member Accounts. New blogs start with them on; an upgraded blog starts with them off.
  • Visitors only see the "Sign in" link once the blog's email address is filled in under Blog Settings, because the sign-in links are sent by email. Blog Options and Members tell you when it's missing.
  • Once signed in, a member sees a small round picture with their initials in the menu, like most sites. Clicking it opens My account, where they can change their details, see their bookings and sign-ups, download their data, delete their account, or sign out.
  • Booking and event sign-up confirmation emails invite people without an account to create one. The link opens the sign-in window with their address filled in, and their earlier bookings and sign-ups are already there.
  • Block signs a member out everywhere and stops them signing in until you unblock them. They aren't told.

Pictures

Members can upload their own picture in My account (JPG, PNG, GIF or WebP, up to 5 MB). It replaces their initials in the menu. You see it on their page in Members, in the Member Log, and in the Visitor Log. If a picture isn't suitable, click Remove picture on their page; their initials show again.

Shown on the Site

Someone in Members can have a public profile: a picture, a biography, links, and a form that emails them. Their email address is never shown. That's how an event's host can be someone who doesn't sign in to the admin site. On their page, click Show on the site, or Edit their profile once they have one. Members shown on the site can then be chosen as an event's host, next to your users.

Deleting Someone, and Their Data

Download their data saves a file with everything the blog keeps about the person: their account, bookings, sign-ups and forms with their answers, email subscriptions, comments and sign-ins. Send it to them if they ask what you have about them.

Delete everything deletes their account (they're signed out everywhere), their email subscriptions, their picture and their profile on the site. On past bookings, sign-ups and forms, their name, email, phone and answers become "Deleted person"; the dates and amounts stay for your records. Comments they wrote stay as they are. It can't be undone.

It waits while they have an upcoming booking, a place at an upcoming event, or host an event. Their page lists what to do first.

The Member Log

Member Log on the admin home page lists every time a member signed in, newest first: who, their IP address, their browser, how they signed in, and when. The Sign-ins button on a member's page shows just theirs. The Visitor Log also shows signed-in members by their picture and name.

Gotchas

  • People are matched by email address. Someone who books with one address and signs up with another shows as two people.
  • A sign-in link works once, for 15 minutes. A member who waits too long asks for a new one.
  • Only a member's visits after they sign in are linked to them in the Visitor Log.

See Also

  • The Admin Site and User Management
  • Bookings and Booking Pages
  • Events and Sign-Ups
  • Subscribers and Email Notifications

PAGES.TITLE: Taking Payments with Stripe
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Connect your own Stripe account to take payments for bookings and events: keys, the webhook, test mode, deposits, tax and refunds.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog takes payments for bookings and paid events through your own Stripe account. The money goes straight to you; Galaxie Blog takes no cut. This page covers connecting Stripe, testing it, and refunds.

Table of Contents

  • Connecting Stripe
  • The Webhook
  • Testing First
  • Currency and Tax
  • Deposits and Paying the Rest
  • Refunds
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Connecting Stripe

Open Blog Options > Payments. In your Stripe dashboard, under Developers > API keys, copy the keys into the Stripe test keys and Stripe live keys sections:

  • Publishable key (starts with pk_)
  • Secret key (starts with sk_ or rk_)
  • Webhook signing secret (starts with whsec_), from the webhook below

A saved secret shows as "Saved, ..." with its last four characters; leave the box blank to keep it. The status line says when you're ready to take payments, or what is still needed.

The Webhook

Stripe tells your blog when a payment goes through, so the booking or the event place is confirmed. In Stripe, under Developers > Webhooks, add an endpoint with your blog's address followed by /common/services/stripeWebhook.cfm, and these events: checkout.session.completed, checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded, checkout.session.expired and charge.refunded. Copy its signing secret into the Webhook signing secret box.

Testing First

Leave Test mode on while you try it. Pay with the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242, any future date and any three digits; no real money moves. Turn test mode off to take real payments; that needs all three live keys.

Currency and Tax

Currency: every price on the blog is in this currency. Tax: your prices include tax, or tax is added at checkout with a name (for example "Sales tax") and a rate.

Deposits and Paying the Rest

A booking type can be paid online in full, by a deposit online (an amount or a percentage), or at the session. With a deposit, the rest is paid at the session (you mark it paid in Bookings) or online, through a "Pay the rest" link in the reminder email. A paid event is always paid in full when people sign up.

Refunds

Refunds are automatic when a client cancels early enough: at least the booking type's (or the event's) Refunds hours before the start. Otherwise refund from the booking or the event's sign-ups, in full or in part. Cancelling a booking or a sign-up yourself can refund too. Refunds made in the Stripe dashboard also show on the booking.

Gotchas

  • Without the webhook, payments go through in Stripe but your blog never hears about them, so places and bookings aren't confirmed.
  • A deposit is only used when it's more than 0 and less than the price; otherwise the full price is charged.
  • A time or an event place is only held for about half an hour while someone pays, then it's free again.

See Also

  • Bookings and Booking Pages
  • Events and Sign-Ups
  • Settings and Options, Explained

PAGES.TITLE: Bookings and Booking Pages
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Let visitors book a time with you: booking types, locations, hours, booking pages, approvals, emails and your calendar.
PAGES.BODY:
Bookings let visitors book a time with you: a consultation, a session, a lesson. You set up where you meet, what can be booked, and when you're available. Visitors pick a time on a booking page, and you approve, change or cancel bookings from the admin site. Paid bookings go through your own Stripe account.

Table of Contents

  • Getting Started
  • Booking Types
  • Locations
  • Hours
  • Booking Pages
  • What Visitors See
  • Handling Bookings
  • Emails and Your Calendar
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Getting Started

Click Bookings on the admin home page. The buttons are in the order you'll use them day to day: Bookings, Calendar, New booking page, Booking types, Locations and Hours. To start taking bookings:

  1. Set up your Booking types, Locations and Hours.
  2. Click New booking page to make a page where visitors book.

Times are in your blog's time zone, set in Blog Settings. Visitors see them in their own time zone.

Booking Types

A booking type is something that can be booked, for example a free 25-minute consultation or a one-hour session. Each one has:

  • Name, an optional Category to group types, and a Description clients read before they choose a time.
  • Length, how often Start times fall, and Time between bookings before and after.
  • Booking: one-on-one, or a group where several people can book the same time, up to a group size.
  • Locations: where it happens. With more than one, clients choose.
  • Price (0 is free) and Payment: paid online in full, a deposit online, or paid at the session. For a deposit, the rest is either paid at the session or online from the reminder email. Refunds sets how many hours before the start a client who cancels gets their money back.
  • Notice (how soon it can be booked), Book ahead (how far ahead), Per day (a limit), and a Reminder email some hours before.
  • Approve first: the time is held, and the client is told it's confirmed once you approve it.
  • Questions: an optional form from Forms. Name and email are always asked.

Locations

A location is how you meet: in person (with an address and an "Open in maps" link), online (one link every time, or a link you email before each meeting), or by phone (you call them, or they call you). Add instructions such as parking or which door. Locations are shared with Events.

Hours

Set your general hours for each day of the week, and different hours for a location if you like. Under "Days off, different hours and busy times", close a day, change its hours, or block part of it. A time is only offered when you're free: you're treated as one person, so a booking of any type at any location takes that time, including the time between bookings.

Booking Pages

A booking page is a page with your text and the booking form under it. It stays up, isn't dated, isn't in your RSS feed, and doesn't show comments or a byline. Click New booking page, give it a title, and after Next choose what it Offers: all booking types, one category, or a single type. Make it an ordinary page takes the booking form off and keeps the page and its text.

To add bookings to a page you already have instead, open the page and choose Insert > Booking (or the calendar button in the editor's toolbar). The editor shows the booking choices the way visitors see them. Bookings can't be added to blog posts, because a booking stays available; it belongs on a page.

What Visitors See

  1. The booking types under their categories, each with its length, price, description and a Book button. With only one type, this step is skipped.
  2. How they'd like to meet, when the type has more than one location.
  3. A calendar with the free days, in their own time zone (they can change it), and the free times for the day they pick. A month with no free times says so above the calendar.
  4. Their details and your questions. Signed-in members have theirs filled in.
  5. For a paid booking, Stripe's payment page. The time is held while they pay.
  6. "You're booked", or, when you approve first, "Thank you - your request is in".

Their confirmation email has a calendar file and a Cancel or change this booking link, where they can move or cancel it until it starts.

Handling Bookings

  • Bookings lists upcoming, past or all bookings, and how many are waiting for your approval. Bookings are never deleted.
  • Open a booking to Approve it, Cancel booking (with a note to the client and an optional refund), Mark completed or Mark no-show (for your own records), mark the rest as paid, refund a payment, and keep private Notes.
  • Calendar shows your bookings by month, week or day.
  • Everyone who books appears in Members.

Emails and Your Calendar

You get an email, with a calendar file, for every new booking or booking request, and when a client cancels, moves or pays the rest. Clients get emails when they book, when you approve or cancel, and a reminder before the session. Their confirmation also invites them to create an account when member accounts are on.

Under Your calendar in the Bookings window, add your private calendar address to Google, Outlook or Apple Calendar to see your bookings there. Make a new address stops the old one working, for example if you shared it by mistake.

Gotchas

  • A booking type needs at least one location, so set up a location first.
  • Reminder emails are sent by a scheduled task that runs every 15 minutes.
  • Without Stripe keys, clients see the price and pay at the session.

See Also

  • Events and Sign-Ups
  • Forms: Ready-Made or Your Own
  • Members: Everyone in One List

PAGES.TITLE: Events and Sign-Ups
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Turn a post into an event with a date, time and place, take free or paid sign-ups, and handle them from the admin site.
PAGES.BODY:
An event is a blog post with a date, time and place: a class, a workshop, a meetup. Visitors see an event card with everything they need, can add it to their calendar, and can sign up, for free or by paying online. This page covers setting one up, what visitors see, and handling the sign-ups.

Table of Contents

  • Making an Event
  • The Event Window
  • Sign-Ups
  • Paid Events
  • What Visitors See
  • Handling Sign-Ups
  • The Events Page and Calendar Feed
  • Postponing or Cancelling
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Making an Event

Create a new post and, under Blog post:, choose Event. After Next, the event window opens on top of the post editor so you can add the date, time and place. To turn an existing post into an event, open it and choose Event in its Blog post: row.

The post editor shows a preview of the event card, headed "How visitors see it, below the post's picture:". The Event details button reopens the event window. Saving in the event window saves the event straight away; you don't need to save the post as well.

The Event Window

  • Status: Scheduled, Postponed or Cancelled. Postponed or cancelled shows clearly on the event card.
  • When: the start and end, or All day. The times are in the event's own time zone, and visitors also see them in their own time zone when it's different.
  • Where: check every location people can attend, for example in person and online. With more than one, people say which when they sign up. Locations are shared with Bookings; Set up locations adds one.
  • Organizer: A person, This blog, or Someone else. A person can be one of your users, or someone in Members who's shown on the site; their name on the event opens their profile, with a form that emails them. Add a person adds someone new, for example a presenter.
  • Cost and Tickets link: optional. A tickets link, for tickets sold on another site, shows as a button on the event card.

Sign-Ups

To let people sign up, choose a Sign-up form. Set up forms makes the blog's own sign-up form the first time (name, email address and notes) and opens it so you can change it. The form shows on the event card, and each person gets a confirmation email with a calendar file and a link to cancel.

  • Capacity counts people, not sign-ups: someone coming with two friends takes 3 places. When it's full, the form is replaced by "This event is full". Leave it empty for no limit.
  • Ask how many people are coming lets each sign-up bring guests, up to Most per sign-up.
  • Sign-ups close 24 hours before the event unless you change it, to give you time to plan food or seating. Set it to the start time to take sign-ups until the event starts.

Paid Events

Enter a Price per person, and people pay online through Stripe when they sign up. Their place is held while they pay and confirmed once the payment goes through. Refunds sets how many hours before the start a cancelled place is still refunded (24 unless you change it; 0 for no refunds). Payments must be set up first; see Taking Payments with Stripe.

What Visitors See

  • On the post: the event card, below the post's picture: when (also in the visitor's own time zone), where, who's hosting, the price, Add to Google Calendar and Download .ics, and the sign-up form. After the end time it says "This event has ended."
  • On the front page: an event with a picture gets a small calendar page on it, and one without a picture gets a date tile. A strip under the title shows when, where and the price.
  • Search engines can show it as an event, and new-post emails to subscribers start with its details.

Handling Sign-Ups

Open Events from the admin home page, then Sign-ups for the event. You see who's coming, how many people, how they'll attend, and what they paid. Export to CSV downloads the list.

  • Add a sign-up is for someone who signed up by phone, by email or in person. Their place is confirmed straight away, even when sign-ups are closed or the event is full.
  • Cancel frees their places, refunds anything paid online in full, and emails them that the organizer cancelled it.
  • People who sign up appear in Members, and their confirmation email invites them to create an account when member accounts are on.

The Events Page and Calendar Feed

Your blog has an Events page at /events: a month calendar with the event days marked, what's coming up, and recent past events. Visitors can subscribe in their calendar app with the calendar feed. The Upcoming Events pod in the sidebar shows the next five events; switch it off in Themes if you don't want it.

Postponing or Cancelling

Change the Status to Postponed or Cancelled. Saving as Cancelled while people are signed up offers to cancel all their places at once: each person is emailed, and anything paid online is refunded in full. A cancelled event hides the calendar buttons, Sign up and Tickets.

Gotchas

  • The sign-up form needs an Email field. Don't also insert the same form into the post with Insert > Form.
  • An event with paid places can't be removed until those people are cancelled and refunded.
  • Only released posts appear on the Events page, the pod and the calendar feed.
  • There's no waiting list: a full event stops taking sign-ups.

See Also

  • Bookings and Booking Pages
  • Taking Payments with Stripe

PAGES.TITLE: Forms: Ready-Made or Your Own
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Place a ready-made form as it is, change it with Edit this form, or build your own: fields, choice limits, sign-up lists and submissions.
PAGES.BODY:
Forms let your visitors send you something: a question, a quote request, a sign-up, a testimonial. Galaxie Blog comes with a dozen ready-made forms you can place in a post or page as they are, without building anything. When you want to change one, or make your own, the form editor is there.

Table of Contents

  • Placing a Ready-Made Form
  • The Ready-Made Forms
  • Changing a Form
  • Building Your Own Form
  • Public Sign-Up Lists
  • Submissions
  • What Visitors See, and What Gets Emailed
  • Spam Protection
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Placing a Ready-Made Form

  1. Open the post or page in the editor and put the cursor where the form should go.
  2. Click the Form button in the editor's toolbar, or choose Insert > Form.
  3. In the Form dropdown, pick one of the Ready-made forms, for example Contact or Request a quote. Type to search the list.
  4. Click Insert.

That's all. The form works as it is: what people send is emailed to the blog's email address, a thank-you message is already written, and the spam check is on. In the editor, the form shows the way visitors will see it, under a small "Form: how visitors see it" label. Move or delete it like any other paragraph.

A ready-made form is created the first time you place it. From then on it is listed under Your forms in the same dropdown, and in the Forms window, so you can place the same form on other pages too.

The Ready-Made Forms

  • Contact: name, email address, subject and message.
  • Newsletter signup: first name, email address, and an agreement to receive emails.
  • RSVP: name, email address, whether they're coming, the number of guests and notes, with a public sign-up list.
  • Potluck sign-up: what each person is bringing, with limits per dish (for example 4 desserts) and dietary notes, and a public sign-up list.
  • Request a quote: what they need, a budget range and when they need it.
  • Feedback: a rating, what they liked and what could be better.
  • Testimonial: their experience, and their permission to publish it.
  • Volunteer sign-up: how they'd like to help, and when they're available.
  • Class or workshop registration: their experience level, and anything you should know.
  • Help request: what happened, and how urgent it is.
  • Guest post idea: a proposed title and summary, and a promise it's their own work.
  • Waitlist: an email address, what they're interested in, and an agreement to be emailed.

A ready-made form you already use, or one with the same title as one of your forms, isn't offered again. Events have their own sign-up form; see Events and Sign-Ups.

Changing a Form

In Insert > Form, choose the form and click Edit this form. The form editor opens. You can also open it from Forms on the admin home page, with Edit. Change the wording, add or remove fields, choose where messages are sent, and click Save. Every page showing the form shows the new version.

A form keeps its address in posts (shown as "Placed in posts as") when you change its title, so pages that show it keep working.

Building Your Own Form

Open Forms and click New form. Start from one of the ready-made forms, or the Blank form, then change anything before you save.

  • Fields are shown in the order listed. Use the arrows to move a field and the X to remove it. Nothing is saved until you click Save.
  • Field types: Text (one line), Email address, Phone number, Number, Text (several lines), Dropdown, Choose one (radio buttons), Choose any (checkboxes), Date, and Consent checkbox. Each field can be required, and can have a placeholder and help text.
  • Choice limits: for a dropdown, radio or checkbox field, tick "Limit how many people can pick each choice". Visitors see how many spots are left, and a full choice can't be picked.
  • Button text and Confirmation message: what the button says, and what visitors see after sending. Or send them to a page of your own with Or go to this page.
  • Email each submission to: one or more addresses, separated by commas. Leave it empty to use the blog's own email.
  • Offer subscribing: adds "Email me new posts" at the end of the form. Someone who ticks it is sent the usual confirmation email, and only becomes a subscriber after confirming.
  • Ask for the captcha: the text-in-an-image check. It can't be read with a screen reader, so you may want it off on a form everyone must be able to use; the form has other spam protection either way.
  • Active: an inactive form isn't shown and doesn't accept anything.
  • Show on: pick posts and pages where the form appears below the text, instead of placing it with Insert > Form.

Public Sign-Up Lists

Some forms are more useful when people can see who else signed up, like a potluck. Turn on Show sign-ups publicly, then tick Show in the public sign-up list on the fields to show. Email and phone fields are never shown. When placing the form, Insert > Form then offers the form, the form and its sign-up list, or the list on its own.

The list updates as people sign up. To leave someone out of it, hide their sign-up under Submissions; it still holds its spot under any choice limits.

Submissions

Everything people send is kept under Forms > Submissions, newest first. Export to CSV opens in Excel or any spreadsheet. Deleting a submission removes it for good and frees its spot under any choice limits. People who send a form also appear in Members, matched by their email address.

What Visitors See, and What Gets Emailed

Visitors see the form in the page, with required fields marked with an asterisk. After sending, the form is replaced by your confirmation message, or they go to your page. Signed-in members have their name, email and phone filled in for them.

You get an email for each submission, with every answer. A plain form doesn't email the visitor. They only get an email when they tick "Email me new posts" (the subscription confirmation), or when the form is an event's sign-up.

In subscriber emails and the RSS and Atom feeds, where a form can't work, it becomes a link to the post.

Spam Protection

Every form is protected, with or without the captcha: a hidden field that only bots fill in, a check that the page wasn't sent too quickly or too long after it opened, and a limit of 10 forms an hour from one connection.

Gotchas

  • Deleting a form deletes its submissions too. Export them first if you want to keep them.
  • If the email to you fails, the submission is still saved under Submissions, and the visitor still sees the thank-you message. Check your mail settings in Blog Settings if messages stop arriving.
  • Hiding a submission keeps its spot under a choice limit; only deleting frees it.

See Also

  • Members: Everyone in One List
  • Subscribers and Email Notifications
  • Email and Comments

PAGES.TITLE: Forms, Events, Bookings, and Members, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How forms, events, bookings, payments and members fit together in Galaxie Blog, and where to read more about each.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can do more than publish: it can take sign-ups, bookings and payments, and keep track of everyone who uses them. This page shows how the pieces fit together, and where to read more about each one.

Forms

Forms let visitors send you something. Place one of the dozen ready-made forms (Contact, Request a quote, Feedback, RSVP and more) with Insert > Form, and it works as it is; click Edit this form to change it, or build your own. See Forms: Ready-Made or Your Own.

Events

An event is a blog post with a date, time and place. Visitors see an event card, add it to their calendar, and sign up, for free or by paying online. Your blog gets an Events page and a calendar feed. See Events and Sign-Ups.

Bookings

Bookings let visitors book a time with you. Set up booking types, locations and hours, then make a booking page. You approve, move or cancel bookings in the admin site, and see them on a calendar. See Bookings and Booking Pages.

Payments

Paid bookings and paid events go through your own Stripe account, with deposits, tax and refunds. See Taking Payments with Stripe.

Members

Everyone who books, signs up, subscribes or sends a form is in one list, Members, matched by email address. With member accounts on, they can sign in with an emailed link (no passwords) to see their bookings and sign-ups in one place. See Members: Everyone in One List.

How They Work Together

  • Locations are shared by bookings and events.
  • A booking type can ask the questions from one of your forms, and an event's sign-ups use a form.
  • A person shown on the site in Members can host an event.
  • Booking and sign-up confirmations invite people to create an account, and signed-in members have their details filled in everywhere.

PAGES.TITLE: Pods, Calendar, and Archive
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The small boxes in the sidebar: the calendar, the archives, recent posts and comments, and the other pods.
PAGES.BODY:
Pods are the small blocks in the sidebar. This page explains what each pod does, how to turn it on or off, and the reason the calendar and archive pods are built the way they are.

Table of Contents

  • What Are Pods?
  • The Pods You Can Use
  • Turning Pods On and Off
  • How the Calendar Works
  • How the Archives Work
  • How Pods Are Cached
  • Gotchas

What Are Pods?

A sidebar lets a reader find their way around without going to a menu. Pods give you a set of ready-made blocks for the things readers look for most: recent posts, categories, the monthly archive, a calendar, and a way to subscribe. Each pod is independent, so you can use only the ones that help your readers.

The Pods You Can Use

The sidebar holds these pods, in this order:

  • Download is a sidebar block. Its text is set in its own section of Pod Content.
  • Subscribe invites readers to subscribe to new posts by email.
  • CfBlogs.org Feed aggregates posts from the CfBlogs community feed.
  • Pages lists your pages.
  • Page Collections lists the page collections featured on the homepage.
  • Recent Posts shows the latest posts.
  • Recent Comments shows the latest comments.
  • Category Archives lists your categories.
  • Monthly Archives lists posts by month.

The calendar is its own pod. It highlights every date that has a post, so a reader can click a day to see what was written.

Turning Pods On and Off

Each pod has an Enable checkbox. You find these on the Themes & Content screen, where each pod's settings sit beside its checkbox. A pod that is off is not drawn, and it costs nothing to leave it off.

Settings for each pod live with the pod. The Recent Posts pod, for example, has its own count, and the Download pod has its own text. Open the pod's section to change them.

How the Calendar Works

The calendar reads every date that has an active post and marks those days. That is why a calendar day can look different after you release a post. A new post appears on the calendar once it is released.

How the Archives Work

The Category Archives pod lists every category. The Monthly Archives pod lists posts grouped by month. Both are cached for a day, so a new post can take up to that long to appear in them unless the cache is cleared. Saving a post clears the archive caches for you, which is why most changes show right away.

How Pods Are Cached

Each pod is stored as a cached file. Saving a post clears the pod files that depend on it, including the archives, the recent posts, the recent comments, and the pages. If a pod still shows old content, reload the page first, then use the refresh options described in Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • A pod can be on but empty. The Page Collections pod, for example, stays empty until you have a visible collection.
  • Pods are cached. A change can take a moment to appear, so check after a refresh before assuming a problem.
  • Too many pods make the sidebar long. Keep the ones your readers use and turn off the rest.

PAGES.TITLE: Popular Posts and Related Blogs
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The scrolling strips of posts on the homepage and under a post: how they choose posts, and how to use the arrows.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog shows two lists of posts that help readers keep going: Popular Blogs on the front page, and Related Blogs at the end of each post. They do different jobs and are computed in different ways. This page explains both.

Table of Contents

  • How Popular Posts and Related Blogs Differ
  • Popular Blogs
  • Related Blogs
  • How to Choose Good Related Posts
  • Gotchas

How Popular Posts and Related Blogs Differ

A reader who arrives on the front page wants to know what other people are reading, so Popular Blogs answers that question for the whole site. A reader who has just finished one post wants the next most relevant thing, so Related Blogs answers that question for one post. Splitting them keeps each list honest about what it is.

Popular Blogs

Popular Blogs appears on the front page only. Each post is scored by its view count divided by the number of months since it was posted, plus one. That formula favors posts that are both viewed and recent, so an old post with many views does not stay on top forever. The list shows the highest-scoring posts, up to twelve.

The list is cached for a day, separately for desktop and mobile views. Saving a post clears the cached copies of this list, so a new post appears once the cache is refreshed.

Related Blogs

Related Blogs appears at the bottom of each post. It is not computed from the content. Instead, it uses the related posts you choose by hand in the post editor, in the Related Posts box. The box shows the placeholder Select Related Post....

The relationship works in both directions. If Post A lists Post B as related, Post B also shows Post A on its own page. Only released posts appear to visitors who are not signed in, and removed posts never appear. Pages cannot have related posts, because they are not part of the post stream.

How to Choose Good Related Posts

Pick two or three posts that a reader would genuinely want next. Good pairs share a topic, a tool, or a question. Avoid adding every post on a theme, because a long list is harder to use than a short one. Since the relationship is two-way, a single choice gives both posts a link.

Gotchas

  • Related Blogs is manual. A new post will not appear in other posts' related lists until you add it.
  • Popular Blogs favors recent posts. A new post with a few views can outrank an older one, which is by design.
  • Removing a post removes it from both lists. Check the related posts of the posts that linked to it.

PAGES.TITLE: Configure Page Collections
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The admin screen that lists every page collection, its status, and its pages, with the tools to add pages, change the hero image, and set the order.
PAGES.BODY:
The Page Collections screen is where you create, arrange, and maintain collections. This page covers each part of it and the reason behind it, so you can manage collections without guessing.

Table of Contents

  • Why Collections Have Their Own Screen
  • Opening the Screen
  • Creating a Collection
  • The Collection Detail Window
  • Adding Pages
  • Deleting a Collection
  • Gotchas

Why Collections Have Their Own Screen

A collection is a group of pages, and it has its own title, hero, theme, and member list. Those settings are not part of any one page, so they live on a screen of their own. That keeps the page editor focused on writing, and it gives you one place to see every collection and its status.

Opening the Screen

Choose Page Collections from the admin menu. The screen lists every collection with its member count and status. Click a row to expand it in place, which shows the details without leaving the list.

Creating a Collection

Click + New Page Collection. The form asks for a title, a description, a hero image, and an optional external URL. An external URL turns the collection into a cross-link to another site. It drops the two-page minimum to one, and the link goes to that address instead of a collection page.

The collection's address is created from its title when you first save it. Changing the title later does not change the address, so the link stays stable.

The Collection Detail Window

Open a collection to edit its details. The fields are:

  • Hero Image (doubles as this collection's icon). The image shows at the top of the collection and on listings.
  • External URL. Makes this a cross-link to another site.
  • Theme. Sets the look of this collection's own listing view.
  • Show in the top menu. Lists this collection in the top menu's collections menu. That menu only appears when at least one collection is checked. See Configure Menu.
  • Members (drag to reorder). The list of pages in the collection, in display order.

An open link called open Pages jumps to the member pages, so you can add or remove members.

Adding Pages

You can add pages from the collection, using Add Pages to Collection. This adds the chosen pages to the end of the list without removing anything. You can also add a collection from the page's own editor, which is the other way a page joins one.

Deleting a Collection

Deleting asks you to confirm with Delete this page collection? Deleting a collection does not delete its pages. The pages stay where they are, and they simply stop being grouped. Remember that any link to the collection itself will stop working.

Gotchas

  • A collection under two pages is hidden, even if it exists.
  • The address is set from the title at creation. Renaming does not change it.
  • Deleting a collection breaks its address. There is no redirect.

PAGES.TITLE: Configure Homepage
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to choose what the homepage shows: featured pages, featured collections, and the blog posts.
PAGES.BODY:
The Configure Homepage screen decides what visitors see first. This page walks through the choices, what each one does, and why the homepage is built from separate sections.

Table of Contents

  • What Are Homepage Sections?
  • Opening the Screen
  • The Three Sections
    • Featured Pages
    • Featured Collections
    • Blog Posts
  • How Saving Works
  • A Plain-Language Summary
  • How to Build a Good Homepage
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What Are Homepage Sections?

A homepage has to do several jobs at once. It should show your newest writing, point readers to your most important pages, and highlight a themed group of content. Galaxie Blog handles that by stacking three independent sections: Featured Pages, Featured Collections, and recent Blog Posts. Each section can be on or off, and each one has its own choices. You can run a blog-only homepage, a landing page with a few featured pages, or a mix of all three.

Opening the Screen

Open the admin site and choose Configure Homepage. The screen has a button labeled Manage Page Collections that opens the collection list, which is where you create and edit collections before you can feature them.

The Three Sections

Featured Pages

Turn on Pages, then pick the pages to feature. The list of pages is saved as a list of page IDs, and it can hold up to 500 characters of IDs. If you pick exactly one page, that page becomes the entire homepage, so think carefully before doing that.

Featured Collections

Turn on Collections, then pick the visible collections to feature. A collection has to have at least two pages, or one page when it has an external URL, before it is available here. If none are ready, the screen tells you that a collection needs at least two pages.

Blog Posts

Blog Posts is always on and cannot be turned off. It shows the recent posts in the number set by your entries-per-page setting, with a View All Posts link under them. Because it is always on, a homepage that only shows posts is the default.

How Saving Works

Saving checks your choices before it writes anything. It refuses a save if Pages is on with nothing picked, if Collections is on with nothing picked, or if any collection you picked is no longer visible. If the save succeeds, the homepage caches are cleared, so the new layout shows on the next visit.

A Plain-Language Summary

The screen shows a short description of what the homepage currently does, such as which sections are on and how many items each one has. Read that summary after each change. It is the quickest way to confirm the homepage matches what you meant.

How to Build a Good Homepage

  1. Create your page collections first, and make sure each one has its pages.
  2. Decide whether the homepage should lead with a landing page (Pages), a themed group (Collections), or your writing (Blog Posts).
  3. Turn on the sections you want, pick their contents, and save.
  4. Open the homepage on a phone and on a desktop, and check that the order makes sense on both.

Gotchas

  • Turning on Pages with nothing selected will not save. Pick a page first.
  • Picking exactly one page replaces the whole homepage. It is the most powerful option here, and the easiest to use by accident.
  • A collection can drop out of the choices if it falls under its minimum of pages. Check the collection list if a collection is missing.

PAGES.TITLE: Page Collections and Homepage Design
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The overview: what a page collection is, how it differs from a page, and how the homepage chooses what to show.
PAGES.BODY:
This page explains the design of page collections and the homepage together. It is the reason the two features work the way they do, and how they relate to each other on your site.

Table of Contents

  • What Are Page Collections?
  • How a Page Joins a Collection
  • How Ordering Works
  • The Two-Page Minimum
  • Hero Images and Enclosures on a Collection
  • How the Homepage Uses Collections
  • How the Homepage Is Cached
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What Are Page Collections?

A blog is built around posts, which are dated and sorted by time. Many sites also have content that is not a post: a portfolio, a set of services, a set of guides. Those pages belong together, but they should not be dated or mixed in with the blog. A page collection is a themed index that links to two or more pages. It is a lightweight group with a title, a description, and a hero image, and nothing else. It has no body, no date, no author, and no comments, because those belong to the pages it links to.

How a Page Joins a Collection

A page joins a collection from the page's own editor, not from the collection. Saving a page replaces the whole list of collections that page belongs to. There is also an additive path, Add Pages to Collection, which adds pages to a collection without removing any existing membership. The page side is the source of truth, so a page always knows where it lives.

How Ordering Works

Members of a collection are listed by their sort order. New members go to the end. You can drag members into a new order in the collection's detail window, labeled Members (drag to reorder), and the new order is saved right away.

The Two-Page Minimum

A collection needs at least two pages before it appears anywhere on the site. The minimum drops to one when the collection has an external URL, because then it is a cross-link to another site and has no member pages to show. A collection below its minimum is not visible, and it is not selectable on the homepage.

When a collection falls under its minimum, for example because you removed a page, Galaxie Blog dissolves it automatically and shows an admin notice. Dissolving a collection does not delete the pages in it. The collection's address simply stops working, and there is no redirect, so check your links after a dissolve.

Hero Images and Enclosures on a Collection

A collection has a hero image. It also doubles as the collection's icon and its card image on listings. A plain hero image is the simplest option. A gradient is another option, and it replaces the hero image. A full enclosure, which can be an image or a video, is edited in the enclosure editor. Video is not offered for collections. When a collection has an enclosure such as a map or a carousel, that enclosure takes priority over the plain hero strings.

How the Homepage Uses Collections

The homepage can show three things, stacked in this order: a set of featured pages, a set of featured collections, and the recent blog posts. Each section is independent and additive, so you can turn on any combination. The homepage settings are saved together, and the save checks that every collection you picked is currently visible. If Pages is on, you must pick at least one page. If Collections is on, you must pick at least one collection.

One special case: if Pages is on and exactly one page is selected, that page's full content becomes the whole homepage. Use this for a landing page you want to control completely.

How the Homepage Is Cached

The homepage sections and the collection lists are cached for a day. Saving the homepage settings clears those caches, so changes show right away. If a change does not appear, use the refresh options in the admin, then see Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • A collection with fewer than two pages is hidden, and it will not appear on the homepage even if you pick it.
  • Dissolving a collection breaks its address. There is no redirect.
  • Page membership is set from the page. Saving a page can remove it from collections you did not touch, so check the page's collection list before saving.

See Also

  • Enclosures: What a Post Shows First
  • Fallbacks and Hero Pictures
  • Themes and Grids, Start to Finish

PAGES.TITLE: Page Collections
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to create a page collection, add pages to it, give it a hero image or gradient, and feature a group of posts with a category link.
PAGES.BODY:
A page collection groups two or more pages under one themed card. This page covers how to create one, what it needs before it shows up, and how to style it.

Table of Contents

  • What Is a Page Collection?
  • Creating a Collection
  • Adding Pages
  • The Hero Image and Gradient
  • Media for a Collection
  • Featuring Posts
  • Breadcrumbs
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What Is a Page Collection?

Visitors do not think in terms of single pages. They think in terms of "show me the portfolio" or "what services do you offer." A page collection matches that way of thinking. It groups the pages a visitor would look at together, gives the group its own landing page, and gives the homepage a single card to link to it. Creating a collection is the way to turn several pages into one section of your site, without building a new menu or a separate site.

Creating a Collection

Open Page Collections from the admin site and create a new collection. Give it a title and a description. The description is used on the card that represents the collection.

To list the collection in the top menu, check Show in the top menu in the collection's editor. Checked collections appear in the top menu's collections menu, which you can rename in Configure Menu.

Adding Pages

Add a collection to a page in the page editor, using the collection selector. A page can belong to more than one collection. A collection is visible on the site only when it has at least two pages.

The Hero Image and Gradient

A collection's hero image is the picture on its card and at the top of its page. If you do not have an image, a gradient works too. The gradient editor lets you pick two or more colors, and an overlay text can sit on top of the hero.

Media for a Collection

A collection can show the same kinds of media as a post. In the collection editor, use the enclosure options to add one:

  • Image: a picture, cropped and optimized like a post image. See Adding an Image to a Post.
  • Video: an uploaded video, or an embedded one. See Video in a Post.
  • Map: a map. This needs an Azure Maps key. See Maps in Posts.
  • Carousel: a rotating set of images.

A collection can also use a gradient as its hero, with optional overlay text. Choose the media that suits the collection, then check its card on the homepage and on the collection's own page.

Featuring Posts

A collection's card can also point at a category, so the card links to the list of posts in that category. This gives a group of posts the same themed card a group of pages gets.

  1. Create a category, and assign the posts to it.
  2. Create a page collection with a title, a description, and a hero image.
  3. Set the collection's External URL to the category's listing link.
  4. Add one page to the collection. A collection with an external URL needs at least one page to show up, instead of two.

Clicking that card opens the category's post list, not a combined page.

Breadcrumbs

Breadcrumbs are the short trail near the top of a page that shows where the reader is. Page collections get breadcrumbs the same way categories do, and there is nothing to set up.

  • A collection's own page shows Home, then Blog, then the collection's title.
  • A page that belongs to a collection shows the collection's title after Home. A page in more than one collection shows each one.

On a phone, the trail on a collection's own page is not shown.

Gotchas

  • A collection with fewer than two pages is hidden, unless it has an external URL, which needs one page.
  • Posts cannot join a collection directly. Use a category with the external URL method above.

See Also

  • Page Collections and Homepage Design
  • Configure Homepage
  • Enclosures: What a Post Shows First
  • Categories, Tags, and Related Posts
  • The Theme Settings and Fonts

PAGES.TITLE: Configure Menu
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The admin screen for the top menu: your own links, the names of the menus, and which page collections appear in it.
PAGES.BODY:
The top menu is the row of links at the top of every page. Since 4.8, Galaxie Blog builds it for you, and the Configure Menu screen sets the parts that are yours: your own links, and the names of the menus. This page explains what is in the menu and how to change it.

What Is in the Top Menu

  • Menu. A link to your blog first, then your own links, then Contact last.
  • Categories. Every category that has posts. It is hidden when there are none.
  • Collections. The page collections marked Show in the top menu. It is hidden when none are marked, and you can rename it.
  • About. The About this Blog, Biography, and Download windows.
  • Search, and on a desktop, the sign-in icon for the admin site.

On a phone there is less room, so Categories and the collections menu are combined into one dropdown, with a heading for each list.

Opening the Screen

Choose Configure Menu from the admin site. It needs the same capability as Themes, since the menu is part of the site's look. Your changes show as soon as you save, for every visitor.

Your Own Links

Use Menu links for links of your own in the Menu dropdown, such as links to your other sites. Click Add a link, then fill in:

  • Label. The text in the menu.
  • Address. It can start with http://, https://, / for a page on this site, or mailto:.
  • New tab. Opens the link in a new browser tab.

Use the arrows to change the order, and the X to remove a link. Your blog's own link always comes first, and Contact always comes last.

Menu Names

  • Collections menu. The name of the menu that lists your collections. Leave it blank for "Collections".
  • Phones (categories and collections). The name of the combined dropdown on phones. Leave it blank for "Explore".

Showing a Collection in the Menu

Which collections appear is set on each collection, not on this screen. Open the collection in Page Collections and check Show in the top menu. A collection that is not visible on the site, for example one with too few pages, is not listed. See Configure Page Collections.

Coming From an Older Version

Before 4.8, Blog Settings had a single parent site link for the menu. The 4.8 update moves that link into Configure Menu, so your menu keeps it. Until you save your own links, the menu goes on showing that parent site link.

Gotchas

  • A custom Navigation Menu template replaces all of this. If you saved a Navigation Menu content template in Themes, the blog shows your own list instead, and the Configure Menu settings do not show. See The Windows and the Navigation Menu.
  • An empty menu is hidden. Categories and the collections menu only appear when they have something in them.

  • Page Collections
  • Configure Page Collections
  • Configure Homepage
  • The Windows and the Navigation Menu
  • Updating Galaxie Blog

PAGES.TITLE: Installing Galaxie Blog
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Installing Galaxie Blog for the first time, step by step, and the checks the installer makes along the way.
PAGES.BODY:
If you're installing Galaxie Blog for the first time, this walks through it end to end. It installs itself through a short four-screen wizard, with nothing to edit by hand along the way.

Before You Start

Your server needs one of these:

  • Adobe ColdFusion. I develop on ColdFusion 2025 and have also tested on 2023; earlier versions back to 2018 have worked for other users, but I have not personally tested 2016.
  • Lucee. I develop and test on Lucee 7.1, and it also runs on Lucee 6.2.

You also need a database: Galaxie Blog uses the database support built into Adobe ColdFusion or Lucee. Check their current lists for the latest. Tested here: SQL Server, MySQL, and MariaDB on current versions, and PostgreSQL and Oracle on older versions. Try a fresh install on a copy before you use another database. See Adobe's ORM settings for the full list of database dialects that ColdFusion supports. The ORM handles the few database-specific column types (see the Gotchas section). You do not need to create the database tables yourself, but you do need to create the database, and a datasource for it in the ColdFusion or Lucee administrator, before you start. Use a new, empty database, with a name made of letters and numbers only (no dots). The installer checks the datasource before it goes on, and it will not install into a database that already holds a blog.

Download and Extract

Download the current Galaxie Blog zip file and extract it. Uploading it to your server as a zip and extracting it there, if your host allows that, is much faster than uploading thousands of small files one at a time over FTP.

Upload to the Server

Upload the extracted files to your server. Galaxie Blog can live at the root of a site, or in its own folder such as /blog, and it does not need a datasource with a special reserved name: give the datasource any name you like, enter that name in the installer, and the installer writes it into org/camden/blog/blog.ini.cfm in the blog's own folder. This also means you can run more than one blog on the same server, each in its own folder with its own ini file and its own datasource.

Running the Installer (4 Steps)

Open the blog's address in a browser. If it is not yet installed, you land on the installer.

  • Step 1 of 4, Welcome. A short introduction and the same empty-database note as above.
  • Step 2 of 4, Site Info. The site's URL and name.
  • Step 3 of 4, Database. The name of the datasource you created, and the database vendor. The box starts empty. Before going on, the installer checks that the datasource exists, that it connects, and that its database does not already contain a blog. If a check fails, you stay on this screen, with a message that says why.
  • Step 4 of 4, User Profile. Your administrator account: name, email and password. The password is salted and hashed before it's saved, never stored in plain text or in a reversible form. While the installer runs, it keeps these details in the blog's settings file, and it removes the password from that file when the install finishes.

The installer then builds the database tables and the starter data, and opens your new blog's home page. Sign in at /admin with the account you just created.

The first thing to do after signing in: open Blog Settings and fill in the Blog Email Address. The installer leaves it empty, and until it's filled in the blog sends no email at all: no member sign-in links, comment notices, subscriber emails or error summaries. If you leave Mail Server empty, the blog sends through the mail server set in the ColdFusion or Lucee administrator, which most hosts already have set up, so the email address alone is often enough. Then send yourself a test.

Updating an Existing Blog

This article covers a new install. If you already have a Galaxie Blog and are bringing it up to 4.8 from an older version, that's a different process: upload the new files over the old ones, then use the Blog Updates screen in the admin interface, which runs the database update for you. The full steps, and the changes in each version, are in UPGRADING.md in the project's repository.

Gotchas

  • The blog only shows the real startup error if you add ?startupDebug=1 to the address, and you are signed in as an administrator (or the blog is not installed yet). Otherwise, only a generic message is shown, and the real error is written to a log file in the logs folder of ColdFusion or Lucee: galaxieBlogStartup.log when the blog could not start at all, and galaxieBlogErrors.log for other errors.
  • The installer will not overwrite a blog. If the datasource you enter points at a database that already has a Galaxie Blog in it, for example another blog on the same server, the installer stops and asks for a different one. Give each blog its own new, empty database and its own datasource.
  • Restart, or clear the caches, after moving or deleting files. Both ColdFusion and Lucee remember where they found a component and the database mapping, and stale ones can cause confusing errors after you rearrange files on the server.
  • Long text columns are handled for you. Every database vendor names its "long text" column type differently. On first start, DatabaseOrmTypes.cfc rewrites the handful of ORM entities that need one (the post body, comments and similar) to match the database type you chose in the installer. You do not need to copy in different files for different databases.
  • .webp and .vtt need a mime type on IIS. The web.config that ships with Galaxie Blog already adds both, for the image format the media library uses and for video captions.

PAGES.TITLE: Updating Galaxie Blog
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How Galaxie Blog installs and updates itself, so you never edit files by hand for an upgrade.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog does not update its own files. Nothing downloads new code while the blog runs. Updating is a two-part job: you put the new files on the server, then you run a database update from inside the admin site. This page explains why the update works that way, and what each part does.

Why Files and the Database Are Updated Separately

The code is the set of files the site runs on. The database holds your posts, settings, and users. A new release can change either or both. Keeping the file upload and the database update as separate steps means you can see what changed before you run it, and you can stop if something looks wrong. A blog that rewrote its own code in the background would make that check impossible.

Step 1: Put the Files on the Server

Upload the new release's files to your server, replacing the old ones. Do not overwrite your blog's configuration file, org/camden/blog/blog.ini.cfm, since it holds your database connection. The admin's update check repeats this warning.

Back up your database first. If you are updating to 4.8 and your footer shows your own text, copy that text into Themes, Composite Footer in the admin site and save it before you upload the files. In 4.8 the footer built into the blog is a neutral default, and a saved Composite Footer is shown instead of it. See The Composite Footer.

Step 2: Check for a New Version

The latestVersionCheck screen reads a version feed and lists every release newer than the one you have installed. For each release it shows the notes, the bug fixes, and the files changed. It only reads and displays the information. It does not download anything, so you still upload the files yourself.

Step 3: Run the Database Update

Open Blog Updates in the admin site and click Update Galaxie Blog's database. The update runs the version scripts in order. Each script is tied to a release, and the blog saves its version after each one. If a script fails, the run stops there, so you can fix the problem and run the update again without repeating the steps that already worked.

If your database is too old to use the admin site, the blog sends you to a standalone update page instead. That page has the same button and the same behavior.

The 4.8 update also creates the tables that page collections use, and moves the single parent site link from Blog Settings into the new Configure Menu screen, so your top menu keeps that link. Afterward, add any other links in Configure Menu, and check Show in the top menu on the page collections you want in the menu.

What Visitors See During an Update

The blog will not run against a database that is too old for the current code. Until the update finishes, visitors see a page saying the site is being updated, and administrators are sent to the update page. This protects visitors from errors caused by a half-updated database.

Gotchas

  • Upload the files first, then run the database update. Running it against old files will not work.
  • Save your footer before updating to 4.8. Otherwise the neutral default footer replaces your own text until you save it in Themes, Composite Footer.
  • Do not overwrite the configuration file. Your database connection lives there.
  • The update check does not download code. It only tells you what is new.

PAGES.TITLE: URL Rewrites, Explained
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Hiding index.cfm from addresses with a server rewrite rule, and turning on the matching setting in the blog.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can build clean addresses without index.cfm in them, such as /my-post instead of /index.cfm/my-post. That takes two things working together: a setting in the blog, and a rewrite rule on the web server. This page explains both, and why the blog cannot provide the rule itself.

Table of Contents

  • Why Clean Addresses Help Readers and Search Engines
  • The Two Parts
  • What the Blog Ships With
  • When the Setting Takes Effect
  • Testing on Your Own Machine
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Why Clean Addresses Help Readers and Search Engines

Clean addresses are easier to read, easier to share, and easier for search engines to understand. A link ending in index.cfm works, but it looks like a technical detail leaked into your site. Removing it is a small change with a lasting effect on how your posts look in search results.

The Two Parts

The blog side is a checkbox called Server Rewrite Rule in place? on the Blog Options screen. When it is checked, the blog builds every link without index.cfm, and it strips the filename from the sitemap. The web server side is a rewrite rule that takes a clean address and passes it to the blog. The blog cannot add that rule, because the rule belongs to the web server, not the application.

If you check the box without the server rule, every link on the site will break. If you install the server rule without checking the box, the links will still work, but they will carry index.cfm and the clean form will be unused.

What the Blog Ships With

The blog ships a web.config file at its root. It turns off directory browsing, turns on compression, shows detailed error pages, and adds the file types the blog uses, such as WebP images and caption files. It does not contain any URL rewrite rules. The help text on the Blog Options screen tells you to set the rule on the server yourself.

When the Setting Takes Effect

The setting is read when the application starts. After you change it, restart the application or reinitialize it, so the blog picks up the new value. If links look wrong after a change, that is the first thing to check. The troubleshooting page covers how to reinitialize.

Testing on Your Own Machine

A local test server usually has no rewrite rules. Leave the box unchecked there, so the links use index.cfm and work. Turn it on only where the server rule exists, which is normally your live site.

Gotchas

  • Checking the box without the server rule breaks every link. Set the server rule first.
  • The sitemap follows the same setting. It strips index.cfm only when the box is checked.
  • A change needs a restart or reinitialize before it shows.

PAGES.TITLE: Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: When a change does not show up, how to reinitialize or restart the blog, where the error logs are, and how to see a startup error.
PAGES.BODY:
When something on your blog does not look right, start with the simplest fix. Most problems are a stale cache or code that has not reloaded after a change. This page covers the tools for those cases, and where to find the errors.

Table of Contents

  • Where the Blog Stores Error Logs
  • Reinitializing
  • Refresh Site and Reload ORM Objects
  • When You Need to Restart
  • Startup Errors
  • Pages That Do Not Update
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Where the Blog Stores Error Logs

  • Error Log in the admin site lists errors the blog caught. Use the Hits column to see which errors repeat.
  • Send Diagnostics in Blog Options emails the blog owner when a new error happens.
  • The galaxieBlogErrors log file (galaxieBlogErrors.log, in the logs folder of ColdFusion or Lucee) records the errors the blog catches while it runs.
  • The galaxieBlogStartup log file (galaxieBlogStartup.log, in the same folder) records the errors that stop the blog from starting at all, such as a wrong datasource or a database the blog cannot reach.

Reinitializing

Add ?reinit=1 to any address on your blog, for example https://yourblog.example/index.cfm?reinit=1. It resets the application and clears the caches. Use it after you change settings, or move files on the server.

Reinitializing affects every visitor, so the blog only accepts it from a signed-in administrator. It also works while the blog is not yet installed, or when a reinstall has been requested.

Refresh Site and Reload ORM Objects

The admin home screen has two icons for the same job without a URL: Refresh Site clears the caches, and Reload ORM Objects reloads the database mappings. Both need the Manage Settings capability.

When You Need to Restart

Restart the application server, not just the blog, when you have:

  • moved or deleted files on the server
  • changed a database column or a mapping in the code

Both ColdFusion and Lucee remember old component locations until they restart, and a reinitialize does not always clear them.

Startup Errors

If the blog fails to start, visitors see a generic message. To see the real error, add ?startupDebug=1 to the address. The detail appears only for a signed-in administrator, or while the blog has not finished starting. Otherwise, check galaxieBlogStartup.log in the logs folder of ColdFusion or Lucee. When the blog could not start at all, the error is in that file, not in galaxieBlogErrors.

Pages That Do Not Update

Work through these in order: reinitialize, then Refresh Site, then check the page again. For active theme work, turn on Disable Cache in Blog Options, so each change shows at once.

Gotchas

  • Turn Disable Cache off when you finish. It makes the blog slower for every visitor.
  • Reinitialize when traffic is low, since it resets the blog for everyone who is visiting.
