PAGES.TITLE: Install and Admin, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The overview for installing Galaxie Blog, finding your way around the admin site, and configuring the blog.
PAGES.BODY:
This is the complete path from nothing to a working blog: installing Galaxie Blog, signing in to the admin site, setting the blog up, and keeping it current. Read it once from start to finish, then use the links to go deeper on any step.

Table of Contents

  • What You Need Before You Start
  • Step 1: Put the Files on the Server
  • Step 2: Run the Installer
    • What the Installer Writes to Your Settings File
  • Step 3: Sign In and Look Around
  • Step 4: Set Up the Blog
  • Step 5: Keep It Current
  • When Something Goes Wrong
  • Where to Go Next
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What You Need Before You Start

Galaxie Blog runs on a ColdFusion or Lucee server, and it stores its content in a database. You need three things before you begin:

  • A server running Adobe ColdFusion or Lucee. The blog is tested on current versions, and the install page lists exactly what has been tested.
  • A database that the server can reach. SQL Server, MySQL, and MariaDB are tested on current versions. Create a new, empty database, and a datasource for it in the ColdFusion or Lucee administrator. The installer will not install into a database that already holds a blog.
  • The blog's files, downloaded as a zip. Uploading the zip and extracting it on the server is much faster than uploading thousands of small files one by one.

The reason for the empty database is simple. The installer creates its own tables, and it will not safely share a database with another application's tables.

Step 1: Put the Files on the Server

Upload the files to the folder your site uses. The blog can live at the root of the site, such as yoursite.com/, or in its own folder, such as yoursite.com/blog/. Either works. The installer does not ask you to edit any paths, because it works out where it is from where it lives.

If your host allows it, upload the zip and extract it on the server. That keeps the file count low and avoids a long, fragile upload.

Step 2: Run the Installer

Open the blog's address in a browser. If the blog is not installed yet, you land on the installer, which has four screens:

  1. Welcome. A short introduction, and a reminder to use an empty database.
  2. Site Info. The site's address and name. These appear in page titles, emails, and the feed.
  3. Database. The name of the datasource you created, and the database type. Before it goes on, the installer checks that the datasource connects and that its database does not already hold a blog.
  4. User Profile. The first administrator account. Use a strong password. It is salted and hashed before it is saved, so it is never stored as plain text.

When the last screen finishes, the installer creates the tables and the starter content, and opens your new blog. Sign in at /admin with the account you just created.

What the Installer Writes to Your Settings File

The installer records the datasource name and the database type in a small settings file, org/camden/blog/blog.ini.cfm, inside the blog's own folder. Because the settings live in the blog's folder, two blogs can run on the same server, each with its own file and its own database. While the installer runs, it also keeps your administrator details in this file, and it removes the password when the install finishes.

Step 3: Sign In and Look Around

Sign in at /admin. The home screen is a grid of icons, one for each part of the blog. Each icon opens in its own window, so you can keep several open at once. You only see the icons that your role allows. An author, for example, sees Create Post and Posts, but not Blog Settings or Users.

Start with three icons: Blog Settings, for the site's identity and connections, Blog Options, for the technical switches, and Create Post, so you can write something and see it appear. See Settings and Options, Explained and The Admin Site and User Management.

Step 4: Set Up the Blog

Set the basics before you publish anything. Work through these in order:

  • Blog Settings: the site name, the blog email address, the time zone, and the mail server. The installer leaves the blog email address empty, and the blog sends no email until it's filled in: no member sign-in links, comment notices, subscriber emails, password resets or error summaries. Leave the mail server empty to use the one set in the ColdFusion or Lucee administrator. Set it first and send yourself a test.
  • Blog Options: SSL, the rewrite rule for clean links, the image and video limits, and the Azure Maps key if you plan to use maps.
  • Email and Comments: how the branded emails look, and whether you use the built-in comments or Disqus. See Email and Comments.
  • Configure Menu: your own links in the top menu, such as links to your other sites, and the names of the menus. See Configure Menu.
  • The footer: a new blog shows a neutral default footer. Put your own in Themes, Composite Footer. See The Composite Footer.
  • Clean links: if your server can hide index.cfm, set that up, then turn on the matching option. See URL Rewrites, Explained.

Step 5: Keep It Current

When a new version of Galaxie Blog comes out, upload the new files over the old ones. Then sign in and open Blog Updates. When an update is waiting, the icon says so. Each update shows what it changes before it runs, and the blog saves its progress after each step, so a failed update can be started again. See Updating Galaxie Blog.

After you upload files, restart the application server, not just the blog. The server remembers old code until it restarts, and a reinitialize does not always clear it.

When Something Goes Wrong

Most problems fall into three groups. A page that will not load usually means the database or the datasource is wrong, so check the settings file and the datasource in your server's administrator. A change that does not appear usually means a stale cache, so reinitialize or use Refresh Site. A startup error that the visitor cannot see is written to galaxieBlogStartup.log in the logs folder of ColdFusion or Lucee, and other errors to galaxieBlogErrors.log. See Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Where to Go Next

  • Installing Galaxie Blog: the installer screen by screen.
  • The Admin Site and User Management: roles, capabilities, and the user tools.
  • Post Editing, Start to Finish: writing your first post.

Gotchas

  • Use an empty database. A database with other tables in it can cause the installer to fail partway, and the installer refuses a database that already holds a blog.
  • Send yourself a test email early. A mail problem found on day one is much easier to fix than one found the day a post goes out.
  • Restart after moving files. A reinitialize alone can leave old code running.

See Also

PAGES.TITLE: The Admin Site and User Management
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The admin home screen, the icons you see for your role, and how to add users, set roles and capabilities, and handle logins and bans.
PAGES.BODY:
The admin interface is where you manage posts, pages, media, users, comments, themes, and server settings. This page covers the home screen and the user tools.

Table of Contents

  • Getting There
    • The Icons
    • What You See Depends on Your Role
  • Roles
  • Adding a User
  • Passwords and Login History
  • Bans
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Getting There

Sign in at /admin. The home screen is a grid of icons, and each one opens in a window over the same page, so you can have several open at once.

The Icons

For an administrator the icons include Create Post, Pages, Posts, Comments, Categories, Tags, Fonts, Forms, Events, Bookings, Subscribers, Users, Members, User Profile, Themes and Content, Blog Settings, Blog Options, Visitor Log, Ban Visitors, Banned Users, Admin Log, Member Log, Error Log, Reaction Log, Search Queries, Import Data, Blog Updates, Refresh Site, and Reload ORM Objects.

The Blog Updates icon shows "(update needed)" when the database is behind the blog's version. See Updating Galaxie Blog.

What You See Depends on Your Role

You only see the icons your role or capabilities allow. An Author, for example, sees Create Post and Posts, but not Blog Settings or Users.

Roles

  • Administrator: everything.
  • SuperUser: everything except server and database settings.
  • Author: create and edit their own posts.
  • Editor: edit and make posts, and adjust categories and related posts.
  • Designer: edit theme settings, and add images to posts.
  • Moderator: edit or remove comments, and ban users.
  • Subscriber: upload photos in their own comments, and edit their own profile.
  • Guest: view posts and comment, without uploading media.

You can also give a user individual capabilities, or build a custom role. The capabilities include Create Post, Manage Images, Manage Categories, Manage Comments, Manage Files, Manage Pages, Edit Posts, Edit User Profile, Manage Settings, Manage Subscribers, Manage Templates, Manage Themes, Manage Users, and Schedule and Release Posts.

Adding a User

Click Create New User at the top of the User grid. Every field except the website is required, and the user name must be unique. The password you enter is only used for their first sign-in. A branded email then asks them to finish their profile and choose their own password.

Passwords and Login History

Passwords are salted and hashed before they are saved, so nobody can look one up, including an administrator. A user who forgets their password needs their own access to change it from their profile. To see a user's logins, open their profile and click Login History.

Bans

Ban Visitors bans by IP address or by User-Agent. Banned Users lists who is banned, when, and by whom. Both need the Manage Users capability.

Gotchas

  • Passwords cannot be recovered. Plan support around that.
  • Invite links do not expire. Treat an unused invite like any other credential.
  • Guest and Subscriber are working roles. Guests can comment, and Subscribers can also comment with photos.
  • Users and Members are different. Users run the blog and sign in here. Members are everyone else, the people who book, sign up, subscribe or send a form; they never have access to the admin site. See Members: Everyone in One List.

PAGES.TITLE: Search Engines and Feeds
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How Galaxie Blog helps search engines find your posts with a sitemap, and how readers follow your blog through its RSS and Atom feeds.
PAGES.BODY:
Search engines find your posts through a sitemap.Readers and feed readers follow your RSS or Atom feed. This page explains what the blog provides for each, and where you control them.

Table of Contents

  • How Search Engines Find Your Pages and Posts
  • The Sitemap
  • Keeping a Test Site Out of Search
  • The RSS and Atom Feeds
  • Pages and Blog Posts in the Feeds
  • Verification Tags
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

How Search Engines Find Your Pages and Posts

A sitemap is a list of every address on your site, with a note for each one. It helps a search engine find new posts quickly, instead of waiting to stumble on them through links. Galaxie Blog generates the sitemap for you, so it stays current as you publish and remove content.

Search engines do more than find pages. They decide what each page is about, and they show a title and short description in the results. Galaxie Blog gives you the controls for most of that:

  • Titles. A post's title is what most search results show first. Write one that says what the post is about, and keep it distinct from your other titles.
  • Descriptions. The Description field is used for cards and search previews, and it can hold up to 1,250 characters. Write a sentence a reader would want to see in a result, not the first paragraph copied over.
  • Addresses. A short, readable address tells both readers and search engines what a page is about. Galaxie Blog builds addresses from the title, and you can change them in the post's Alias window. See Post URLs and Redirects.
  • Links between your pages. Related posts, page collections, and the homepage all link your content together. Search engines follow those links to find and rank everything.
  • Released content only. Posts that are still pending or have been removed are left out of the sitemap, so search engines only see what readers can see.

The Sitemap

The sitemap lists the blog's front page, every post, and every page. It is generated as XML. The blog's robots.txt file points search engines to it, so most crawlers will find it without any setup. If you use Galaxie Blog's clean addresses, the sitemap uses the same clean form. See URL Rewrites, Explained.

Keeping a Test Site Out of Search

A test or staging site should not appear in search results. Galaxie Blog handles this with a setting called Production Site, found under Blog Settings. When it is not checked, every page carries a noindex tag, which tells search engines to skip it. Check the box on your live site, and leave it off everywhere else.

Tag pages carry their own noindex tag, because they repeat content from posts and do not add much to search.

The RSS and Atom Feeds

Every page links to both feeds through standard tags, so feed readers can discover them on their own. The RSS feed is at /rss.cfm (RSS 2.0) and the Atom feed is at /atom.cfm (Atom 1.0). Both list the same posts and accept the same options you can add to the address:

  • mode sets how much of each post appears. full includes the whole post and short includes a summary.
  • mode2 filters the feed by day, by month, or by category.
  • category and tag filter the feed by a category or tag ID, for example atom.cfm?category=15.

Feed readers that check for updates get a quick “not changed” reply when nothing new has been posted. Most feed readers accept either format. Use the Atom address for a service or reader that asks for Atom.

Pages and Blog Posts in the Feeds

Galaxie Blog has two kinds of content, and they behave differently in the feeds. Pages are built for evergreen content, such as an about page, a service description, or a guide that stays true for years. They are not meant to change often.

Blog posts are for dated content: news, updates, and anything you write at a particular moment. Posts are what a feed reader expects, so both feeds include blog posts only. A new page does not appear in the feed, even when it is released. You can also leave a single post out of the feed by turning off its display-on-feed setting, which is useful for a post you want on the site but not in readers' inboxes.

The sitemap is different. It lists both pages and posts, so search engines can find evergreen pages as well as new posts.

Verification Tags

The blog does not have a field for Google or Bing site-verification tags. To verify your site with those services, add the verification tag through the Custom Header Script panel in Theme Settings. Google Analytics and the Bing Maps key are separate settings, and neither one verifies your site.

Gotchas

  • Turn on Production Site on the live site. A site without it is marked noindex.
  • Both feeds list the same posts. A post turned off for the feed is left out of RSS and Atom alike.
  • Verification tags go in the header script, since there is no dedicated field.

  • Releasing, Promoting, and Removing a Post

PAGES.TITLE: Email and Comments
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The emails Galaxie Blog sends with your branding, and how to switch comments to Disqus.
PAGES.BODY:
Email is how the blog keeps readers and administrators informed. It sends subscriber mail when you release a post, notifies people when a comment is approved, and reports errors when you turn on diagnostics. This page explains how the email settings work and which emails go out.

Table of Contents

  • What Email the Blog Sends and Why
  • The Mail Settings
  • Which Emails Go Out
    • Subscriber Email
    • Comment Notices
    • Error Diagnostics
  • Comment Settings
  • Testing Email
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What Email the Blog Sends and Why

A blog works best when readers come back. Subscriber email is the simplest way to bring them back, and comment notices let commenters know when a conversation continues. Diagnostic email tells you about problems you might not otherwise see.

The Mail Settings

The mail settings are on the Blog Settings screen. They are:

  • Mail Server, the address of your outgoing mail server.
  • Mail User Name and Mail Password, if your server needs them.
  • Mail Failto Address, where undeliverable mail goes.
  • Blog Email Address, the address emails are sent from.
  • CC Email, an address that receives a copy.

The blog will not send email if the Blog Email Address is blank, and a new install starts with it blank, so fill it in before you test anything. If Mail Server is blank, the blog sends through the mail server set in the ColdFusion or Lucee administrator.

Which Emails Go Out

Subscriber Email

When you save a released blog post in the post editor, the blog asks whether to email subscribers. Choosing yes sends the post to every verified subscriber, every time. If the post was emailed before, the prompt asks whether to send it again, which is useful after a major revision. A post scheduled for a later date is emailed automatically when it goes live, so there is no prompt for it. Pages are never emailed.

Comment Notices

When a comment is approved, the blog emails the people who subscribed to that post's comments. The subscribe option appears on the comment form.

Error Diagnostics

If you turn on Send Diagnostics in Blog Options, the blog emails you about errors: by default as one summary a night, or, if you choose Right away, for each new error under Error emails, as they happen. A sudden burst of errors always sends one email right away. See Taming a New Galaxie Blog's Error Log.

Comment Settings

Each post has an Allow Comments checkbox in the post editor. Turning it off stops new comments on that post. Each comment has a Moderated checkbox, which you can use to mark a comment you have reviewed. When a commenter is not signed in and moderation is on, their comment waits for approval before it appears.

Testing Email

Send yourself a test by subscribing with your own address. The subscription sends a confirmation email, and you must confirm it before the address counts as a subscriber. If the confirmation does not arrive, check the mail server, the sending address, and your spam folder, in that order.

Gotchas

  • A blank Blog Email Address stops all sending. Fill it in first.
  • Saying yes to the email prompt always sends, even for a post that was emailed before. Say no if you only fixed a typo.
  • Subscribers must confirm. An unconfirmed address does not receive post emails.

PAGES.TITLE: Settings and Options, Explained
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Blog Settings for the site identity and connections, and Blog Options for the technical switches, panels, and API keys.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog has two places for configuration, and they answer different questions. Blog Settings describes who the blog is and how it connects to the outside world. Blog Options controls how the blog behaves. This page walks through both screens, explains why each setting exists, and tells you what to check when you change one.

Table of Contents

  • Blog Options vs Blog Settings
  • Blog Settings, Step by Step
    • The Main Block
    • Parent Site
    • Server Time Zone
    • Database Connectivity
    • Mail Server Settings
  • Blog Options, Step by Step
    • The Main Block
    • jQuery and Kendo
    • Logging
    • Analytics and Sharing
    • Maps
    • Media and Fallbacks
    • Disqus, Greensock, and Other Libraries
  • Troubleshooting a Setting That Does Not Take Effect
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Blog Options vs Blog Settings

Settings are about identity and connections: your name, your time zone, your database, and your mail server. These change rarely, and a mistake can stop the blog from working, so they sit on their own screen. Options are about behavior: caching, minifying, limits, and third-party libraries. These change more often, and most take effect as soon as you save them.

Blog Settings, Step by Step

Open Blog Settings from the admin home screen. The main block is at the top, followed by four collapsible panels.

The Main Block

  • Site name and blog email. The name appears in titles and emails. The email is the sender for the blog's messages.
  • Production Site. Leave this unchecked while you build or test the blog, so a staging copy is not indexed by search engines by mistake. Check it when you go live.

Parent Site

If your blog sits under a larger site, enter that site's name and address here. The blog uses them to link back to the parent site from its menu.

Server Time Zone

Set the time zone the server runs in. Post dates, release times, and scheduled posts all use it. A post set for 9 a.m. goes out at 9 a.m. on the server's clock, so check it if your server is in another zone.

Database Connectivity

The datasource name, user name, and password are saved in the blog's settings file. The password is stored, not hashed, because the blog needs the real value to connect. Treat this screen like any place that holds a real credential, and limit who can open it.

Mail Server Settings

The outgoing mail server and the sender addresses are used for comment notices, contact messages, password resets, invitations, and error emails. If you change them, send yourself a test message. See Email and Comments.

Blog Options, Step by Step

Open Blog Options. It has a short block of checkboxes at the top and several panels below. Here is what each one does and why you might change it.

The Main Block

  • Use SSL. Check this once your site has a valid certificate. Disqus and some embedded media need SSL to work correctly.
  • Server Rewrite Rule in Place. Check this only after your server hides index.cfm from addresses. The blog builds its links to match, so the box must match the server. See URL Rewrites, Explained.
  • Defer Non-Essential Scripts. Loads some scripts after the page appears, so the first view is faster.
  • Minimize Code. Strips extra whitespace and comments from the main pages before they are sent. It makes pages smaller and faster, at the cost of harder-to-read page source.
  • Send Diagnostics. Emails the blog owner about errors. Error emails show the failing address, the message, and where it happened, but never form values.
  • Error emails. A nightly summary (the default) sends one email a night with every error since the last one, new ones first; Right away, for each new error emails each new error as it happens, rate-limited. Send it after sets the summary's time, and Send a summary now sends one straight away. A sudden burst of errors still sends one email right away. See Taming a New Galaxie Blog's Error Log.
  • Disable Cache. Turns off the page cache. Use it while you change a theme, and turn it off again afterward, because it slows the site for every visitor.

Member Accounts

Lets visitors sign in with a link the blog emails them, to see their bookings and sign-ups in one place. New blogs start with it on, upgraded blogs with it off. Visitors only see the Sign in link once the blog email is filled in under Blog Settings, because the sign-in links are sent by email. Keep signed in sets how many days a member stays signed in on a device. See Members: Everyone in One List.

Payments

Connects your Stripe account, for paid bookings and paid events: the currency, tax, test mode and your keys. See Taking Payments with Stripe.

jQuery and Kendo

These settings choose where jQuery loads from, and which Kendo library the blog uses. Check Commercial Kendo UI Edition only if you have licensed Kendo UI and installed it on the server. Otherwise the blog looks for files that are not there. Then set Kendo Folder Path to the web address of the folder that holds Kendo's js and styles folders, from the site root. For example, /blog/common/libs/kendo/2021R1/ for a blog in a /blog folder, or /common/libs/kendo/2021R1/ for a blog at the site root. Defer Kendo Commercial on Public Site loads the smaller free library for readers, and loads the larger one only in the admin site.

Galaxie Blog is tested with Kendo UI Professional 2021 R1 (2021.1.119), and with the free Kendo Core that comes with the blog. Use Kendo UI 2020 or later. Earlier versions, such as 2019, draw checkboxes and radio buttons in a different way, so the admin site falls back to the browser's plain ones.

Logging

Visitor logging records page views for the Visitor Log and the ban tools. Choose how long to keep visitor logs, from one month to six, and how long to keep error and administrative logs, up to two years. Shorter retention means a smaller database.

Analytics and Sharing

Enter your Google Analytics ID and any AddThis settings if you use them. Leave them empty if you do not.

Maps

Paste an Azure Maps key into the Azure Maps panel to embed maps and routes in posts. Without a key, map features do not work. Bing Maps is kept for blogs with an existing Bing Maps account, but new setups should use Azure Maps. See Maps in Posts.

Media and Fallbacks

The media panel holds the image compression default, the image and video size limits, and the No-Image Fallback setting. The fallback decides what a post shows when it has no picture. See Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

Disqus, Greensock, and Other Libraries

The Disqus panel turns on Disqus comments and holds its identifier. See Email and Comments. The Greensock panel is for the animation library, if your theme uses it.

Troubleshooting a Setting That Does Not Take Effect

Some settings apply right away, and some need the application to restart. If a change does not appear, try these in order: reload the page, use Refresh Site in the admin, reinitialize with ?reinit=1 while signed in, and restart the application server as a last step. See Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • Keep the rewrite box and the server in step. A mismatch produces links that return not-found errors.
  • Turn off Disable Cache when you finish. It is useful while you work, but it makes the site slower for everyone.
  • Do not check Commercial Kendo UI unless you installed it. The site will look for files that are not on the server.
  • Leave the Kendo Folder Path empty unless you use the commercial edition. Empty means the Kendo Core that comes with the blog. It is only required when Commercial Kendo UI Edition is checked.
  • Point Kendo Folder Path at Kendo UI 2020 or later. If you keep several Kendo versions on the server, check that the path names the newest one. With a 2019 folder, the admin site's checkboxes and radio buttons look plain.

PAGES.TITLE: Maps in Posts
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Adding an Azure Maps key, embedding a map or a driving route in a post, and how map previews appear on cards.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can place a map or a route inside a post. Maps use Azure Maps, so the first step is connecting your own Azure Maps key. This page explains why the key is needed, how to add a map or a route, and how the blog shows maps on listing pages.

Table of Contents

  • What the Azure Maps Key Pays For
  • Adding a Map
  • Adding a Route
  • How a Map Appears
  • Why Cards Use Still Map Images
  • A Good Way to Use Maps
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What the Azure Maps Key Pays For

The map data and the route calculations come from Microsoft's Azure Maps service. Azure requires an account and a key for every request, so the blog cannot provide one for you. Your key identifies your account, and it lets you control your own usage and cost. Enter the key in Blog Options, in the field labeled Azure Maps API Key. Without it, the map features will not work.

Adding a Map

In the post editor, open the Insert menu and choose Map. The map window lets you set the location and the zoom level, and choose a style. The styles are road, grayscale dark, night, road with shaded relief, satellite, and satellite with road labels. The zoom level is saved as a whole number, so small changes are rounded.

Adding a Route

Choose Map Directions from the Insert menu to build a route. You choose a travel mode, which is car by default, or bicycle, bus, motorcycle, or pedestrian. Then you enter the stops along the route. The form holds up to sixteen stops, and two is the minimum. Pick a route style the same way you pick a map style.

The route follows the road between the stops, using the travel mode you picked. The live map on the post and the card picture both draw that same road path.

How a Map Appears

A map placed in the body of a post appears where you put it, in a frame about 768 pixels wide and 432 pixels tall.

A map saved as the post's main picture, the enclosure, is shown at the top of the post. Saving a map or a route as the enclosure removes any picture, video, or carousel the post had, because a post has only one enclosure. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

Why Cards Use Still Map Images

A listing page can show many posts at once. A live, interactive map on every card would load a large number of maps, most of which no reader would touch. Galaxie Blog instead fetches a single still image of the map, road path included, the first time it is needed, and saves it on your server. Every card then uses that saved image, so listing pages stay fast. The live map appears only on the post itself.

If the still image cannot be fetched, the blog removes the partial file and tries again later. A missing still image usually means the key is wrong or the service could not be reached.

A Good Way to Use Maps

  • Use a map to show a place a reader needs to find, such as an office or a trailhead.
  • Use a route for a trip with a clear order of stops.
  • Choose a style that stays readable at small sizes, since the card picture is small.

Gotchas

  • No key, no map. Enter the Azure Maps key in Blog Options first.
  • A route follows the road for the travel mode you chose. Change the travel mode to change the path, then check the card picture, since it is saved once and rebuilt after the route is saved.
  • Saving a map as the enclosure removes the picture. Save the picture somewhere else in the post if you want to keep it.

PAGES.TITLE: Fallbacks and Hero Pictures
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What a post shows when it has no photo: the four fallback modes, the hero image pool, and the hero cover image.
PAGES.BODY:
Not every post has a picture, and a post without one can look empty in a list. The No-Image Fallback setting decides what a post shows in its picture spot when it has no picture of its own. This page explains the choices and why each one exists.

What Readers See When a Post Has No Picture

A listing of cards looks uneven when some cards have a picture and some have a blank space. A fallback fills that gap with something deliberate. It is also what appears when you share a post that has no picture, so a fallback shapes how your posts look on social networks too.

The Options

The setting is labeled No-Image Fallback on the Blog Options screen. It has five choices:

  • Generic shows the standard placeholder picture. This is the default.
  • Generated creates a gradient for each post as an SVG image file, drawn in the blog's theme colors. The file is made once and saved on your server. Each post gets its own, so the listing does not look repetitive.
  • Pool Photo picks a photo from a pool you supply. The same post always gets the same photo, so a reader who returns sees no change.
  • Animated Background shows a live animation on the post's own page only. Listings and phones show a still image instead. See Animated Heroes with Vanta.
  • None leaves the picture area empty.

The Pool

The pool option has two settings. Pool Display chooses between a rotating carousel and a single picture. Pool Image Count sets how many pictures the carousel shows. The pool holds up to 75 pictures. Because each post picks by its own ID, the choice is steady, not random.

The Hero Cover Image

A post can have a hero cover image: a single photo you upload for the post that does not replace its live animation or gradient. It shows on listing cards, in the admin list, and as the picture shared on social networks. On the post's own page, a gradient or an animation still plays as chosen. This lets you show a real picture on cards while keeping the live look on the post itself.

How the Choices Are Ranked

When a post is displayed, the blog checks its picture sources in order. A real picture, video, map, or carousel comes first. A chosen gradient or animation comes next. The hero cover image is used on cards and in shares. If none of those exist, the No-Image Fallback applies.

A Good Default

For most blogs, the generated gradients give the best result without any work. They look intentional, they cost nothing to produce, and every post looks different. Use the pool when you have a photo style you want to repeat, and use none only when you prefer a text-only list.

Gotchas

  • The generated gradients are SVG image files, saved on your server, not live CSS, even though the option label mentions CSS.
  • The animation shows only on the post's own page, on desktop. Listings never show it.
  • A chosen gradient or animation replaces the post's picture enclosure. You cannot show both.

PAGES.TITLE: Image Optimization and WebP
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The automatic crops every uploaded image gets, the compression slider, video upload size, and how WebP is used when the server supports it.
PAGES.BODY:
Every picture you upload is processed before it appears on your site. The blog makes copies sized for each place a picture appears, and it can save them in WebP, a format that loads faster. This page explains why each step exists and what you control.

Table of Contents

  • What Happens to Each Picture You Upload
  • What You Can Upload
  • The Copies the Blog Makes
  • WebP
  • Quality
  • Thumbnails and Caching
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What Happens to Each Picture You Upload

A photo straight from a camera is often several megabytes, far larger than a web page needs. Sending that to every reader slows the page and wastes their data. Processing the picture once, at upload, means readers download a file sized for the screen they are using.

What You Can Upload

The blog accepts JPEG, GIF, PNG, and WebP pictures. Each file can be up to 25 megabytes. The upload screens show a cropping tool, so you can frame a picture before it is saved. If a file is too large, the blog rejects it after upload, so check the size first. Your server's own limit on the size of a form post also applies, which is why the blog's help text mentions it.

The Copies the Blog Makes

Each picture you use as a post's main picture gets several copies, sized for where it will appear:

  • A thumbnail for admin lists and small previews.
  • Facebook copies for shared links, in the shared size and the link sizes.
  • Twitter copies for large and small link cards.
  • Google copies in 16:9, 4:3, and square shapes, for search results.
  • Pinterest copy, made only when the original is large enough to fill it.
  • Classic copy, a standard 4:3 image used as a fallback.

Each social network wants a different shape, so one picture is never right everywhere. Making these copies by hand takes time and is easy to forget. The blog makes them for you, so a shared link looks right on every platform.

WebP

WebP is a modern format that is smaller than JPEG at the same quality. Where your server can create WebP files, the blog saves WebP copies of the social sizes too. Lucee can always do this. ColdFusion can do it on the 2025 release and later. If your server cannot create WebP, the blog offers a tool to swap in a WebP version you prepared yourself.

Quality

Quality controls the trade-off between file size and sharpness. The site-wide default is set in Blog Options under Default Image Quality, and it ranges from 0.1 to 1.0, with a default of 0.8. Each upload has its own slider, labeled Image Quality (smaller file to higher quality), which starts at the site default. Quality is applied to JPEG and WebP files. A lower setting makes a smaller file, and a higher one keeps more detail.

The default of 0.8 is a good balance for most photos. Raise it for detailed images such as screenshots of text, and lower it for large photos where size matters more than fine detail.

Thumbnails and Caching

Thumbnails are 235 pixels wide and 138 pixels tall. Like the other copies, they are generated once at upload. Because the copies are files on your server, they are served directly, and that is what makes them fast.

Gotchas

  • Pictures over 25 megabytes are rejected. Resize them before upload.
  • The Pinterest copy is skipped for small originals. That is expected, not a failure.
  • Raising quality makes files larger. Set the default with your readers' connections in mind.

PAGES.TITLE: Enclosures: What a Post Shows First
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What an enclosure is, how to add or replace one in the Enclosure Editor, and the order a post uses to choose its main picture.
PAGES.BODY:
A post's enclosure is the main thing it shows first: a picture, a video, a map, a carousel, a gradient, or an animation. Only one can be the enclosure at a time. This page explains why, how the blog chooses what to show, and what each choice removes.

Table of Contents

  • Why a Post Has One Main Picture
  • The Types
  • How the Blog Chooses What to Show
  • What Each Choice Removes
  • How to Choose Well
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Why a Post Has One Main Picture

A post opens with one strong visual, the thing a reader sees before the words. Showing two competing headers would confuse the page, and a card in a list has only one place for a picture. Limiting a post to one enclosure keeps the top of every post clear, and it means the card and the post always agree.

The Types

  • An image you uploaded.
  • A video, either one you uploaded or a YouTube or Vimeo link.
  • A map or a route.
  • A carousel of images that rotates.
  • A gradient, a color background you choose.
  • An animation, a live background on the post page.

How the Blog Chooses What to Show

On the post's own page, the blog checks the enclosure in a fixed order. A picture, video, or carousel comes first, then a map, then a gradient, then an animation. Because saving one type clears the others, a post normally holds only one of them at a time, so the order rarely matters. If none is set, the blog uses the No-Image Fallback.

Listing pages and admin thumbnails use their own order, and they add the hero cover image as well. That is why a card can show a different picture from the one at the top of the post, if you set a hero cover image.

What Each Choice Removes

Choosing a type clears the others that conflict with it:

  • An image or video clears any map or carousel.
  • A map clears the picture, video, and carousel.
  • A carousel clears the picture, video, and map.
  • A gradient clears the picture, video, map, carousel, and any animation.
  • An animation clears the picture, video, map, carousel, and any gradient.

The hero cover image clears nothing, which is why it can sit alongside any of these.

How to Choose Well

  1. Pick the picture that best represents the post, since it also appears on cards and in shares.
  2. Check the card on the front page after you save. A picture that looks good at the top of the post can crop badly on a card.
  3. Use the hero cover image when you want a real picture on cards but the live look on the post.

Gotchas

  • Saving a new enclosure removes the old one. Save a copy of anything you may want back.
  • The enclosure is the card and share picture. Check the card after you change it.
  • A gradient or animation replaces the picture. You cannot show both at the top of the post.

PAGES.TITLE: Galleries and Carousels
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to show several pictures in a post: an image gallery that readers browse, and a carousel that rotates on its own.
PAGES.BODY:
Galleries and carousels show several pictures together. A gallery lets readers click through a set of thumbnails. A carousel rotates through pictures on its own. This page explains when to use each, how many pictures you can add, and how they are built.

Table of Contents

  • Gallery or Carousel: Choosing Between Them
  • Adding Pictures
  • Building a Gallery
  • Building a Carousel
  • As the Main Picture
  • A Good Set of Pictures
  • Gotchas
  • Built With

Gallery or Carousel: Choosing Between Them

A gallery suits a reader who wants to look closely: a set of photos from a trip, a product in several angles. A carousel suits a quick showcase, where the pictures tell a short story or highlight a few items. Choosing the right one matters more than the look, because a carousel moves on its own, and a reader who wants to study a picture will be interrupted.

Adding Pictures

The upload window lets you add up to twelve pictures in one batch. For a larger set, add a batch, save it, and add another. A gallery can hold up to sixteen pictures, and a carousel can hold up to twenty items. Large pictures are scaled down so their longest side is at most 1920 pixels, and JPG and WebP pictures are compressed. See Image Optimization and WebP. See Image Optimization and WebP.

Each picture in a gallery needs a title of at least four characters. Give each one a short, specific title, since the title appears with the picture.

Building a Gallery

Insert a gallery from the Insert menu, then add the pictures. The gallery shows thumbnails in a grid. Readers click a thumbnail to see the picture larger, and they can move between pictures with arrows or the keyboard. The grid's height adapts to the number of pictures, up to twelve.

Building a Carousel

Insert a carousel from the Insert menu, then add its pictures. The carousel offers a set of transition effects, and it includes a random option that picks one for you. Pictures move with arrow buttons and clickable dots, and the carousel can be driven by the keyboard.

A carousel rotates automatically. The timing of each change is set by the slider library the blog uses, so check how it feels on the post before you release it, rather than relying on a fixed number.

As the Main Picture

A gallery or carousel can be the post's enclosure. Choosing one clears any other main picture, video, or map, because a post has only one enclosure. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

A Good Set of Pictures

  • Use pictures of the same shape and style, so the set looks deliberate.
  • Keep titles short and specific.
  • Choose a set of six to twelve pictures for a gallery. Fewer feels thin, and more is harder to browse.

Gotchas

  • The twelve-picture limit applies to each upload batch. Add more by repeating the upload.
  • A gallery holds at most sixteen pictures, and a carousel at most twenty items. For a longer set, split it into more than one gallery or carousel.
  • Titles need at least four characters. Short titles are rejected.
  • A carousel moves on its own. Keep its pictures simple enough to read as they change.

Built With

Galleries open each picture in an enlarged view using GLightbox, which is MIT licensed. Carousels use Swiper, which is also MIT licensed. See Software and Licenses.

PAGES.TITLE: Media and Maps, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Media and Maps, Start to Finish
PAGES.BODY:
This is the complete guide to media in Galaxie Blog: pictures, video, maps, galleries, and the animated backgrounds. It explains what each kind of media does, where to add it, and what the blog does to it once it is uploaded.

Inline Media vs the Main Picture

Media does two different jobs in a post. Some media sits inside the text, such as a picture next to a paragraph. Other media is the post's main picture, the enclosure, which appears at the top of the post and on the card. The blog keeps those two jobs in two places. The body editor handles the inline media, and the Enclosure Editor handles the main picture. That way, a large hero image or a video does not get in the way of your writing.

The Main Picture: The Enclosure

The enclosure is the large picture, video, map, or carousel that opens the post. It is also what readers see on the card, and what gets shared on social media. Set it in the Enclosure Editor. Choose what kind of media to use, then upload, embed, or build it. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

Pictures

Pictures are the most common media. You can add them inline in the body, or as the enclosure. Common web image formats work. When you upload a picture, the blog creates optimized copies for Facebook, Twitter, Google, and the blog's own pages, so each one looks right where it appears. See Adding an Image to a Post and Image Optimization and WebP.

How Social Crops Are Made Automatically

A picture that looks good in a post often looks wrong in a link preview, because each platform wants a different shape. Making those crops by hand is slow and easy to forget. The blog makes them when you upload, so the picture is ready for every place it appears.

Video

You can embed a YouTube or Vimeo video, or upload your own file. Uploaded video can have a cover image and WebVTT captions. See Video in a Post.

Maps and Routes

Maps use Azure Maps, so the first step is an Azure Maps key in Blog Options. Once the key is in place, you can insert a map, or a route with two or more stops, from the editor. On cards, a map shows as a static picture, which keeps listing pages fast. The full map appears on the post. See Maps in Posts.

Why Cards Show a Still Map

A card page can show many posts at once. A live map on each card would load many interactive maps, and most of them would never be touched. A static picture gives the reader the location at a glance, and the live map waits for the post itself.

Galleries and Carousels

When you have several pictures to show together, use a gallery, where readers click through the thumbnails, or a carousel, which rotates through the pictures on its own. See Galleries and Carousels.

Animated Backgrounds

A post can open with a live animated background instead of a picture. The animation plays on the post's own page, on desktop. Cards and phones show a static gradient, so the listing pages stay fast. See Animated Heroes with Vanta.

When a Post Has No Picture

Not every post needs a picture. The No-Image Fallback setting decides what a post shows instead: a plain placeholder, a generated gradient, a photo from your pool, or nothing. The fallback is set once for the whole blog, and it applies to every post without a picture. See Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

Size Limits

Large uploads can fail. The limits for images and videos are set in Blog Options, and the defaults allow typical photos and short videos. For a very large video, hosting it yourself and linking to it is often easier. Check the limits before a big upload, so the failure does not happen halfway through.

Gotchas

  • The enclosure is the card picture. Check the card after you change it, not only the post.
  • Maps need the Azure Maps key. Without it, the map features do not work.
  • A gradient or animation replaces the enclosure. Choosing one removes the picture, so you cannot show both.

See Also

  • Image Optimization and WebP
  • Fallbacks and Hero Pictures
  • Animated Heroes with Vanta
  • Maps in Posts

PAGES.TITLE: Animated Heroes with Vanta
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to choose an animated Vanta background for a post or the whole site, and when the animation runs.
PAGES.BODY:
An animated hero is a live, moving background at the top of a post. It plays on the post's own page on a desktop, and gives a post a look no still picture can. This page explains what the animation is, why it is limited to the post page, and how to choose one.

Table of Contents

  • Galaxie Blog Animation Interface
  • Why Animations Play Only on Post Pages
  • The Effects
  • Adjusting an Effect
  • Choosing One
  • What the Animation Replaces
  • A Site-Wide Default
  • Gotchas
  • Built With
  • See Also

Galaxie Blog Animation Interface

This screenshot is taken from the Enclosure Editor Interface:


Why Animations Play Only on Post Pages

An animation runs continuously and uses the processor. A listing with many animations would slow down every reader and drain phone batteries. So the blog plays the animation only on a single post, on a desktop. Listings, cards, and phones show a still image instead. The post itself gets the full effect, and everything else stays fast.

The Effects

The Effect menu offers nine choices: Birds, Clouds, Clouds 2, Fog, Globe, Net, Rings, Waves, and Random. Random is meant to pick one per post. Check the result on the post's own page before you rely on it, because the Random choice does not always resolve to an effect the way the other choices do.

Adjusting an Effect

Each effect has its own options. The Speed slider runs from 0.3 to 3, with 1 as the normal speed. Most effects let you set colors with swatches, and a set of numeric sliders controls shape and density. For Net and Globe, a Show Dots checkbox adds points to the lines. Mouse, touch, and gyroscope control is turned off, so the animation plays on its own.

Choosing One

Pick an effect whose colors match the post's theme, and keep the speed slow. A fast animation can pull attention from the words. Set the effect in the post's hero window, and check the post on a desktop before you release it.

What the Animation Replaces

Choosing an animation removes the post's picture, video, map, carousel, and gradient, because a post has only one main picture. If you want a picture on cards while keeping the animation on the post, use the hero cover image described in Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

A Site-Wide Default

Blog Options has an Animation Effect setting that applies to posts that have no animation of their own, when the No-Image Fallback is set to Animated Background. It also plays only on the post page.

Gotchas

  • Listings show a still image, not the animation. That is by design.
  • Phones do not play the animation. Check the desktop view when you judge the effect.
  • Choosing an animation removes the picture enclosure. Use the hero cover image to keep a picture on cards.
  • Random may not resolve as expected. Verify it on the post before you release.

Built With

The animations use Vanta.js, which draws on three.js. Both are MIT licensed. See Software and Licenses.

The author's own blog runs on Galaxie Blog at gregoryalexander.com/blog/, which is one place to see these features in use.

PAGES.TITLE: Video in a Post
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Adding video to a post: embedding YouTube or Vimeo, uploading your own file, and the older video directives.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can show video in two ways: a video you upload, or a video hosted on YouTube or Vimeo. Each has its own steps, limits, and trade-offs. This page explains when to use each, and how the video player and captions work.

Table of Contents

  • Hosted vs Uploaded Video
  • Embedding a YouTube or Vimeo Video
  • Uploading a Video
  • Captions
  • How the Player Loads
  • Using a Video as the Main Picture
  • Gotchas
  • Built With
  • See Also

Hosted vs Uploaded Video

Hosting a video yourself gives you full control and keeps the video on your site. It also uses your server's bandwidth and storage, and it has a size limit. YouTube and Vimeo carry the bandwidth for you, and they are good at delivering video to many devices. Most blogs use the hosted option for long videos and the upload for short clips they want to keep under their own control.

Embedding a YouTube or Vimeo Video

Paste the video's link into the video window and choose YouTube or Vimeo. The blog plays the video in its own player, with the provider's controls. Embedded videos do not use a cover image, since the provider supplies its own.

Uploading a Video

Upload a video in MP4, WebM, Ogg, QuickTime, or MPEG format. The default size limit is 100 megabytes, and you can change it in Blog Options under media uploads. An upload that is too large is rejected after it arrives, so check the size first.

An uploaded video can have a cover image, which is the picture shown before the video plays. Upload the cover from the video window, using the same cropping tool as other pictures.

Captions

Captions help readers who cannot hear the audio, and they help anyone watching without sound. Upload a caption file in WebVTT format, with the extension .vtt, in the caption window. The captions appear as a track in the player, marked as English. Captions apply only to uploaded videos, not to YouTube or Vimeo, which have their own caption tools.

How the Player Loads

The player is loaded when a video is on the page, not before. The uploaded video starts loading its details first, and the full file loads when the reader plays it. That keeps a post with no video as light as possible.

Using a Video as the Main Picture

A video can be the post's enclosure, shown at the top. Choosing one clears any picture, map, or carousel. Remember that the cover image is what cards show, so set one for an uploaded video if you want a good card picture.

Gotchas

  • Uploaded videos are limited to 100 megabytes by default. Raise the limit in Blog Options, or host a long video elsewhere.
  • Captions apply only to uploaded videos.
  • The cover image is used only for uploaded videos, not for YouTube or Vimeo embeds.

Built With

The video player is Plyr, which is MIT licensed. Plyr loads only when a video is on the page. For the full list of libraries and their terms, see Software and Licenses.

PAGES.TITLE: Why Galaxie Blog?
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What comes built into Galaxie Blog, and why you do not need to buy plugins to get fast pages, a media pipeline, social images, animations, maps, and carousels.
PAGES.BODY:
Most blog software starts with an empty box and asks you to add everything else yourself. Galaxie Blog starts with the things a serious blog needs already in place: fast pages, a media pipeline, social sharing images, animated and map-based content, and the tools to run it all from one admin site. This page explains what comes built in, and why that matters.

Table of Contents

  • What We Are Building Toward
  • A Blog Built for the ColdFusion Community
  • Built In Means Nothing Extra to Buy
  • Fast by Design
  • A Media Pipeline That Does the Work
  • Social Sharing Images, Handled Automatically
  • Carousels, Galleries, and Video
  • Animated Heroes and Maps
    • Animated backgrounds
    • Maps and routes
  • Built In for the Work Around the Writing
  • Portable, and Works With Your Database
  • How the Media Features Compare
  • Where Other Blog Software Is Stronger
  • Costs to Expect
  • Related Links
    • Engines and platforms
    • Other blog platforms
    • Libraries used in Galaxie Blog
    • Licenses
  • Where to Start

What We Are Building Toward

Four goals shape Galaxie Blog. They are aims, not finished claims, and each one shows up in the features described on this site.

  • Speed. Performance is a top goal. Finished pages, pods, card listings, and feeds are cached, and only the parts that depend on a change are rebuilt. Libraries load when a page needs them, so a page with no gallery does not download the gallery viewer.
  • Full functionality. We aim for Galaxie Blog to be one of the most fully functional blog platforms available. Publishing, scheduling, subscribers, comments, search, visitor tools, and a built-in error log all sit in one admin site, so you do not have to assemble them yourself.
  • Unparalleled media support. Images, video, galleries, carousels, maps and routes, and animated backgrounds are all part of the post editor, with the processing that makes them look right on every platform.
  • A blog you can make your own. Built-in themes can be changed in Theme Settings, colors and fonts are set there, and the Kendo theme controls the widgets. You can add your own header script for site-wide changes, and give any single post its own CSS and JavaScript from the editor's CSS and JavaScript buttons.

A Blog Built for the ColdFusion Community

If you already write ColdFusion, Galaxie Blog is the blog platform that speaks your language. It is written in CFML, runs on Adobe ColdFusion and on Lucee, and is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, change it, and run it on your own server. In that sense it is to the ColdFusion community what WordPress is to the wider web: a complete, self-hosted blog you can build on.

Built In Means Nothing Extra to Buy

Many blogs reach a useful state only after adding a stack of plugins. Each one adds a cost, a setup step, and something else to keep updated. Galaxie Blog takes a different approach. The features most blogs have to buy are part of the software, and they work together, because they were built together.

Fast by Design

Speed comes from caching, and Galaxie Blog caches the parts of a page that are expensive to build. Finished post pages, sidebar pods, card listings, RSS feeds, and popular-post lists are saved and reused, so a visitor usually gets a page that is already built. Saving a post clears only the cached pieces that depend on it, so the site stays fresh without rebuilding everything. You do not need a caching plugin to get this. See Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs if you ever need to clear it by hand.

A Media Pipeline That Does the Work

Every picture you upload is processed for the places it will appear. Galaxie Blog makes thumbnails for the admin site, copies sized for Facebook, Twitter, Google, and Pinterest, and a classic version for everything else. Where the server supports it, WebP versions are made too, which load faster. You choose the crop and the quality in the upload window, and the blog handles the rest. See Image Optimization and WebP.

Social Sharing Images, Handled Automatically

When a post is shared, the picture that appears in the preview has to fit each network's shape. Galaxie Blog generates those shapes from the post's picture, so the preview looks right without you resizing anything. A post without a picture can use a hero cover image for shares and cards, or a generated gradient, so even a text-only post looks finished. See Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

Carousels, Galleries, and Video

Galaxie Blog includes carousels, with a set of transition effects, and galleries that open each picture in a full-size viewer. Video can be embedded from YouTube or Vimeo, or uploaded with captions. These are part of the post editor, so you add them in the same place you add a picture. See Galleries and Carousels and Video in a Post.

Animated Heroes and Maps

Animated backgrounds

A post can open with a live animation, such as birds, waves, or a network of lines. The animation plays on the post's own page on a desktop, and listing pages show a still image, so the animation adds character without slowing down the rest of the site. See Animated Heroes with Vanta.

Maps and routes

Maps and driving or walking routes can be placed in a post with Azure Maps. Connect your own Azure Maps key, and the map and route appear in the post, with a still picture on listing pages. See Maps in Posts.

Built In for the Work Around the Writing

The admin site also covers the work that surrounds a blog. You can schedule a post to release later, email subscribers when you release a post, moderate comments, and see which posts and searches get attention. Structured data for search engines is generated for each post, and a sitemap and RSS feed are built in. Visitor logs, error logs, and automatic blocking for known bad bots help keep the site healthy. See Scheduling a Post and How Search Engines Find Your Pages and Posts.

Portable, and Works With Your Database

Galaxie Blog runs today on Adobe ColdFusion and on Lucee, so you can choose the engine that fits your server and budget. Its database layer is built on ORM, which supports a range of databases. The installer offers Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL and MariaDB, and Oracle, along with several other database types. If your database is not in the list, the installer notes that it may still work with a change to the application settings.

BoxLang support is planned and coming soon. It will let the same blog run on a newer CFML-compatible engine, once it is released.

How the Media Features Compare

On WordPress, the features in this section usually come from separate plugins, code snippets, or page-builder add-ons. Animated backgrounds are typically added with a snippet or a builder add-on. Map routes are typically added with a mapping plugin, such as WP Map Block or WP Go Maps. Carousels and social-image handling are typically added with further plugins. Each one needs its own setup and its own updates.

Galaxie Blog combines animated post heroes, Azure Maps routes, carousels, and automatic social-image crops in one open-source, self-hosted package. Other platforms offer some of these features, such as Squarespace's map and animated background blocks, but we did not find another blog platform that includes all of them built in.

Galaxie Blog includes these features in one package, with the same admin site, the same media pipeline, and the same caching. You configure them in one place, and they are kept up to date with the blog itself.

Where Other Blog Software Is Stronger

Galaxie Blog is a smaller project than WordPress, with a smaller community and fewer third-party extensions. If you need a specific feature that only a plugin provides, check first whether Galaxie Blog already has it. If it does not, that is a real limit, and it is worth knowing before you choose.

Costs to Expect

Galaxie Blog is free and open source. The main running costs are your web hosting and, if you use maps, your Azure Maps account, which is billed by Microsoft by usage. Read the Software and Licenses page for the terms of each library.

Related Links

If you want to read more about the tools behind Galaxie Blog, these are good places to start.

Engines and platforms

  • Adobe ColdFusion, the commercial CFML engine, with its documentation.
  • Lucee, the open-source CFML engine.
  • BoxLang, a newer JVM language that Galaxie Blog plans to support.

Other blog platforms

  • WordPress, the most widely used blog software.
  • Squarespace, a hosted site builder with blogging built in.
  • Ghost, a publishing platform focused on writing.

Libraries used in Galaxie Blog

  • Kendo UI Core, the widgets behind the admin site.
  • TinyMCE, the post editor.
  • Uppy, the upload and cropping tool.
  • Swiper, the carousels.
  • Vanta.js, the animated backgrounds.
  • Plyr, the video player.
  • Prism, the code highlighting.
  • Azure Maps, the maps and routes.

Licenses

Galaxie Blog is released under the Apache 2.0 license. See Software and Licenses for the terms of each library.

Where to Start

Install the blog with Install and Admin, Start to Finish, then build the look with Themes and Grids, Start to Finish. When you are ready to write, see Post Editing, Start to Finish.

The author's own blog runs on Galaxie Blog at gregoryalexander.com/blog/, which is one place to see these features in use.

PAGES.TITLE: Galaxie Blog Docs Overview
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What the Galaxie Blog documentation covers, where to start, and how to upgrade a blog.
PAGES.BODY:
This section explains Galaxie Blog from the ground up: how to install it, how to run it day to day, and how to get the most out of its features. It is written for people who run a blog on Galaxie Blog, and for people who are thinking about it. Each page covers one area in enough depth that you can act on it without hunting elsewhere.

How the Docs Are Organized

The docs are grouped into sections that match the admin site. Each section has a start-to-finish overview page, followed by pages on specific features. If you are new, begin with the overview for the section you need, then read the feature pages it links to.

  • Install and Admin covers installing the blog, the admin site, and the settings that run it.
  • Themes and Grids covers the look of the blog, its fonts, the Kendo theme, and the grids you use to manage content.
  • Media and Maps covers pictures, video, galleries, maps, and the animated heroes.
  • Post Editing covers writing and releasing posts, and the tools inside the editor.
  • Homepage and Page Collections covers the homepage, the sidebar pods, and grouping pages into collections.
  • Releases and Upgrades covers release notes and how to update an existing install.
  • Visitors and Safety covers visitor tracking, bans, the error log, and comments and subscribers.

How These Docs Explain Each Feature

A feature is easier to use when you know what problem it solves. Each page here gives the reason a feature exists, then the steps to use it, then the gotchas that have caught people out. Where a behavior is not yet confirmed, the page says so instead of guessing.

Where to Start

If you have never installed Galaxie Blog, start with Install and Admin, Start to Finish. If the blog is already running and you want to change how it looks, start with Themes and Grids, Start to Finish. If you want to write, start with Post Editing, Start to Finish.

Keeping the Docs Accurate

Galaxie Blog changes over time, and so do these pages. When a page and the admin screen disagree, the screen is the truth, and the page should be updated to match. If you find something that does not match what you see, that is worth reporting, because the next reader will hit the same confusion.

Gotchas

  • Admin menu labels can differ slightly from the docs. Use the label on your screen when they do.
  • Some features need a restart or a cache refresh before they show. The troubleshooting page explains how.
  • Some features depend on keys or settings you have to supply, such as an Azure Maps key for maps.

PAGES.TITLE: Release Notes: 4.65 and 4.8
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What changed in Galaxie Blog 4.65, the repository update and fixes, and 4.8 "Bella's Pawtrait Edition", with its animations, fallbacks, and hero images.
PAGES.BODY:
This page covers the two most recent releases: 4.65, which brought the public repository up to date with the working copy, and 4.8 "Bella's Pawtrait Edition," which adds animated heroes and new image fallbacks.

Table of Contents

  • Galaxie Blog 4.8 "Bella's Pawtrait Edition"
    • Animated Heroes
    • What Shows When a Post Has No Image
    • Gradient Heroes
    • Hero Cover Image
    • Social Sharing Images
    • The Top Menu and Configure Menu
    • A Neutral Default Footer
    • A Safer Installer
    • An Atom Feed
    • Subscriber Emails
    • Upgrading to 4.8
  • Galaxie Blog 4.65: Closing the Gap With the Public Repository
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Galaxie Blog 4.8 "Bella's Pawtrait Edition"

Animated Heroes

A post's hero can be a live animated background instead of a photo. Pick one from the Enclosure Editor, or set a site-wide default in Blog Options. The eight effects are Birds, Clouds, Clouds 2, Fog, Globe, Net, Rings, and Waves. Each has its own colors and settings, and a live preview. An optional line of overlay text can sit on top. The animation plays on a post's own page. Cards and listings show a gradient instead.

What Shows When a Post Has No Image

Each post card picks the first of these that applies: a real image, video, map, or carousel; a Hero Cover Image; a gradient hero; an animated background; and finally the site-wide No-Image Fallback setting. See Fallbacks and Hero Pictures.

Gradient Heroes

The overlay text on a gradient hero can be sized from 12 to 72 pixels. The gradient editor also accepts a raw CSS gradient pasted from another tool.

Hero Cover Image

A photo that stands in for a post's gradient or animation on cards and in social-media shares. It never changes the post's own page.

Social Sharing Images

Each social platform tries its own crop first, then the classic crop, then the theme's default logo, and uses the original image only as a last resort.

The Top Menu and Configure Menu

The top menu is now built for you, from your own links, the categories that have posts, and the page collections marked Show in the top menu. The new Configure Menu screen sets your own links and the names of the menus. Phones get one combined dropdown. See Configure Menu.

A Neutral Default Footer

The footer built into the blog is now neutral. Your own footer goes in Themes, Composite Footer, and the version and copyright lines are added under it automatically. See The Composite Footer.

A Safer Installer

The installer checks the datasource before it goes on: it must exist, connect, and point at a database that does not already hold a blog. The datasource box starts empty, so the installer never suggests a name that another blog on the same server may be using. The administrator password is removed from the settings file when the install finishes, and an error that stops the blog from starting is written to galaxieBlogStartup.log.

An Atom Feed

The blog now has an Atom feed at /atom.cfm, next to the RSS feed.

Subscriber Emails

When a post with a table of contents is emailed to subscribers, the table of contents is left out of the email, since its links only work on the page itself.

Upgrading to 4.8

If your footer shows your own text, save it in Themes, Composite Footer first. Then upload the files, open Blog Updates in the admin site, and run the 4.8 update. Restart the application server afterward, so the new code loads.

Galaxie Blog 4.65: Closing the Gap With the Public Repository

The public repository had fallen well behind the working copy. Version 4.65 brought it up to date, comparing the two file by file, and keeping out personal photos, licensed libraries, and stale cache files. Several things changed:

  • Readable table of contents anchors. Headings in a table of contents now get readable links, such as #introduction, instead of random ids.
  • Adobe ColdFusion compatibility. A status text attribute that only Lucee supports was removed, so the site also runs on Adobe ColdFusion.
  • Database deadlock fix. The category listing ran one query per category on nearly every page view. It is now a single grouped query. The same pattern was fixed for tags.
  • Kendo Professional can be deferred. A blog option lets public pages load the smaller Kendo Core, and load the larger library only on the posts that need it.
  • Error log entries can be deleted, not just marked as resolved.
  • A map crash is fixed. A malformed coordinate on an older map no longer throws an error.

Gotchas

  • Restart after upgrading. Files can be updated while the old code keeps running until the application restarts.
  • Some 4.8 behavior is still being checked on live sites, especially the mobile view of animated heroes.

PAGES.TITLE: Release Notes: 4.9
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Galaxie Blog 4.9 "Join the Pack Edition": forms, events, bookings, payments and members.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog 4.9 "Join the Pack Edition" turns the blog into a place where visitors can do things: send forms, sign up for events, book a time with you, and pay. It also brings everyone who does so into one list, Members.

Table of Contents

  • Forms
  • Events
  • Bookings and Booking Pages
  • Payments
  • Members
  • The Admin Site
  • Fixes
  • Upgrading to 4.9
  • See Also

Forms

  • A form editor with ten field types, required fields, choice limits ("4 desserts"), and a confirmation message or page.
  • A dozen ready-made forms, placed as they are with Insert > Form, and an Edit this form button to change one.
  • Forms and booking choices show the way visitors see them inside the post editor.
  • Public sign-up lists, submissions with CSV export, and an optional "Email me new posts" box.

Events

  • A post can be an event, with a date, time, time zone, locations and a host.
  • An event card on the post with Add to Google Calendar and a calendar file, and a calendar page or date tile on the front page.
  • Sign-ups with capacity, guests, a closing time, and paid places; cancel links and owner tools to add or cancel sign-ups.
  • An Events page, a calendar feed, and an Upcoming Events pod.

Bookings and Booking Pages

  • Booking types, locations (in person, online or by phone) and weekly hours with days off.
  • Booking pages: a page with your text and the booking form. Booking is a kind of page, not a blog post.
  • Approval, reminders, cancel and reschedule links, a bookings calendar, and a private calendar feed for your own calendar app.

Payments

  • Stripe payments for bookings and events, with deposits, tax, test mode and automatic refunds.

Members

  • One list of everyone who books, signs up, subscribes or sends a form, with each person's history.
  • Member accounts with an emailed sign-in link and no passwords, My account, and details filled in for members.
  • A round picture with the member's initials in the menu, or their own picture.
  • Public profiles for members who host events.
  • Download their data and Delete everything, for privacy requests.
  • A Member Log of sign-ins, and members shown by picture and name in the Visitor Log.

The Admin Site

  • A cleaner admin look: alternating blocks, aligned labels and clearer headings.
  • New icons: Forms, Events, Bookings, Members and Member Log. People is now part of Members.
  • Choosing a post type is clearer, with Blog post, Page and Collection on their own rows.
  • Admin windows read properly on phones.
  • Error emails come as one summary a night, new errors first, with one email right away if many errors happen at once. Choose it in Blog Options under Error emails.

Fixes

  • The pager no longer runs into an empty "No Entries" page.
  • Social sharing images use full addresses.
  • WebP uploads are only offered where the server can handle them.
  • The Kendo folder path in Blog Options is only needed for the commercial Kendo edition.
  • The Upcoming Events pod sets itself up on databases whose ids don't number themselves, instead of failing on every page.
  • RSS and Atom feeds no longer fail when a post starts with a form or a booking.
  • The Blog Settings window finds the blog's settings file again.

Upgrading to 4.9

Run the update as usual; see Updating Galaxie Blog. The new tables are made for you. Member accounts start off on an upgraded blog: turn them on in Blog Options > Member Accounts, after filling in the blog's email address in Blog Settings. To take payments, connect Stripe in Blog Options > Payments.

PAGES.TITLE: Pods: Customizing the Sidebar
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to change the content of each pod in the sidebar, and how a saved list differs from the automatic one.
PAGES.BODY:
The sidebar on the front page is made of pods. Each pod is a box with a heading and some content, such as a subscribe form, a list of recent posts, or the archives. The heading and its icon come from the blog itself. The Theme Settings screen controls the content inside each box. This page covers each pod and what you can change in it. For how the editor itself works, see Theme Content Templates.

Table of Contents

  • The Pods
  • Changing a Pod
  • Keeping a Pod Up to Date
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

The Pods

Theme Settings lists these pods, each with its own Desktop and Mobile editor and an Enable checkbox:

  • Download Pod. The Download Galaxie Blog box. Its built-in content has the download information and a button.
  • Subscribe Pod. A box that invites visitors to subscribe to new posts. Its built-in content includes the subscribe form.
  • Recent Posts Pod. A list of the most recent posts.
  • Recent Comments Pod. A list of the most recent comments.
  • Category Archive Pod. A list of your categories, each linked to its archive.
  • Monthly Archives Pod. A list of the months that have posts.
  • Calendar Pod. A calendar of posts. It has no saved code, and it is always shown.

Every pod except the Calendar Pod works the same way. If you have saved code, the pod shows it in place of the built-in content. If you have not, the pod shows the built-in content.

Changing a Pod

Open the pod's editor from Theme Settings, using the Desktop or Mobile Edit button. Write your content in the editor and submit it. The heading is not part of the code. It stays in place above your content, so you do not need to add one.

If you want the built-in content back, open the editor and use Discard Changes. The pod then shows its built-in content again.

Keeping a Pod Up to Date

The built-in versions of the Recent Posts, Recent Comments, and archive pods build their lists from your database. Saved code does not do that. If you save a static list, the list stays as you wrote it, and new posts and comments will not appear until you edit it. If you want the list to keep itself current, do not save code for that pod.

Gotchas

  • Saved code replaces the list. A pod with saved code no longer updates automatically. See the section above.
  • Disabling a pod hides it everywhere. The Enable checkbox applies to all themes, so this screen cannot hide a pod on one theme only.
  • The Calendar Pod has no saved code. Its content is generated, so there is nothing to edit in the editor.

  • Pods, Calendar, and Archive
  • Popular Posts and Related Blogs
