PAGES.TITLE: The Composite Footer
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to replace the neutral default footer with your own, what the blog adds under it, and the custom footer scripts.
PAGES.BODY:
The footer is the strip at the bottom of every page. It shows your own Composite Footer, or, until you save one, a neutral default with the footer logo. The footer is a content template with its own Desktop and Mobile editor, and it has its own Enable checkbox. For how the editor works, see Theme Content Templates.

Table of Contents

  • The Footer Logo
  • The Composite Footer
  • Custom Footer Scripts
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

The Footer Logo

The neutral default footer shows the footer logo. In Theme Settings, use the Footer Logo field to upload a logo or to enter the path to one you already have. Once you save your own Composite Footer, it is shown in place of the default, so add a logo to it yourself if you want one there.

The Composite Footer

The composite footer is where your own footer goes. It has a desktop version and a mobile version, each with its own Edit button, and an Enable checkbox. Until you save one, the blog shows a neutral default footer with the footer logo, and, while you are signed in as an administrator, a reminder of where to replace it. Phones show the mobile version. If you only saved the desktop version, phones show that instead.

Under your footer, the blog always adds two lines of its own: the Galaxie Blog version with the theme name, and a copyright line with the current year and the blog's title. You do not need to put either one in your footer.

Custom Footer Scripts

Custom Footer HTML lets you add scripts or other code at the very end of every page. Use it when a service needs a script placed there, for example an analytics snippet. Turn on Apply across all themes if the same code should go on every theme. Leave it off to apply the code to the theme you are editing.

Gotchas

  • The footer changes the whole page. A mistake in the footer code can break the bottom of every page, so check the mobile version too.
  • Save your footer before updating to 4.8. Before 4.8, the site's own text was built into the default footer. In 4.8 the default is neutral, so copy your text into the Composite Footer first.
  • Custom footer scripts run on every page. Only add a script you trust, and remove it when the service it belongs to is no longer used.
  • Disabling the footer removes it everywhere. Use the Enable checkbox only when you want no footer at all.

PAGES.TITLE: The Windows and the Navigation Menu
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to change the About, Biography, and Download windows and the navigation menu.
PAGES.BODY:
Some parts of the site are not in the sidebar. The About, Biography, and Download windows open from the menu, and the navigation menu is the list of links at the top of every page. Each one is a content template with its own Desktop and Mobile editor. For how the editor works, see Theme Content Templates.

Table of Contents

  • The About Window
  • The Biography Window
  • The Download Window
  • The Navigation Menu
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

The About Window

The About window opens from the menu at the top of the page, and it shows information about the blog. It is optional. Uncheck its Enable box to hide it. The window's content is the About Window template, which you edit in the same way as the other parts.

The Biography Window

The Biography window also opens from the menu. Each user can enter their own biography in their user profile, and the Biography Window template sets how the window lays it out. Like the About window, it is optional and has an Enable checkbox.

The Download Window

The Download window opens on the left side of the page when a visitor clicks the menu icon. It holds the download information for Galaxie Blog. Its Enable checkbox hides the window on every page. Its built-in content has the download information, and the Download Pod in the sidebar uses the same kind of content.

The Navigation Menu

The menu at the top of the blog is an unordered HTML list. The outer bullets are the menu items, and the indented bullets inside an item are its submenu. Each item needs an anchor link around its text, or it will not be clickable.

Since 4.8 you rarely need this template. The built-in menu is put together for you from Configure Menu, your categories, and your page collections. Saving a Navigation Menu template replaces that whole menu with your own list, so the Configure Menu settings stop showing.

Use the desktop editor for the desktop menu and the mobile editor for the phone menu. The menu editor's toolbar is limited to undo, redo, link, and lists, and it has no image tools. Test the mobile menu on a phone, since long labels and deep submenus can wrap or run off the screen.

Gotchas

  • The menu needs links. A menu item with no anchor around it will show, but it will not go anywhere.
  • Mobile and desktop menus are separate. A change to one does not change the other unless you use the same code for both.

PAGES.TITLE: Theme Content Templates
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How the content template editor works: the desktop and mobile versions, the theme selector, the Enable checkbox, and how to discard changes.
PAGES.BODY:
Most of the content on your front page is not hard-coded. It is stored as a content template, one per part of the page, and you can edit each one from the Theme Settings screen. A content template can be a pod in the sidebar, one of the windows that open from the menu, the navigation menu itself, or the footer. This page explains how the editor works. The pages after this one explain what each part does.

Table of Contents

  • How a Content Template Works
  • Opening the Editor
  • The Editor
  • The Enable Checkbox
  • Checking Your Changes
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

How a Content Template Works

Every content template has two versions: a desktop version and a mobile version. Each version is stored separately, for each theme. When you save code in one, it replaces the built-in markup for that part on that device. When you have not saved anything, the blog uses its built-in markup, and the editor shows that markup as a sample.

The editor's heading tells you which one you are looking at. A heading that says Current means you have saved code. A heading that says Sample means you have not, and the sample is what the blog shows now.

Opening the Editor

Open Theme Settings from the admin site and find the section for the part you want to change. Each section has an Edit button for the desktop version and another for the mobile version. Click the one for the device you want to change, and the editor opens in a window.

You can change the desktop version and the mobile version separately. If you want the same content on both, use the Apply to Mobile and Desktop checkbox described below.

The Editor

The editor has a text area with a toolbar and a few controls under it:

  • The toolbar. The desktop version has the full set of tools, including styles, lists, links, images, media, the map and map routing tools, custom windows, and emoticons. The mobile version has a shorter toolbar because phones have less room. The navigation menu has the smallest toolbar: undo, redo, link, and lists.
  • Theme(s). Choose one or more themes to receive this code. Pick the themes you want before you submit. An All option is in the list.
  • Apply to Mobile and Desktop. When this is checked, the code is saved to both the desktop and the mobile version.
  • Submit. Saves the code and closes the editor.
  • Discard Changes. Asks you to confirm, then deletes your saved code and returns the part to its built-in markup. You cannot undo this, so copy your code somewhere first if you may want it again.

The Enable Checkbox

Most sections in Theme Settings have an Enable checkbox. Unlike the code, this setting is not per theme. It applies to the whole blog. When it is unchecked, the part is not shown on any theme.

Two exceptions are worth knowing about. The Calendar pod has no saved code and is always shown. The Page Collections pod can appear even when its checkbox is unchecked, as long as it has pages or saved code to show.

Checking Your Changes

Save the code, then load the blog in a browser. Check both a desktop window and a phone-sized window, since the two versions are separate. Some parts are cached, so a change may not show right away. If it does not appear, use the refresh options in the admin, then see Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • Saved code replaces the built-in markup. This includes automatic lists. A pod with saved code shows exactly what you saved, so it will not update on its own when new posts or comments arrive unless your code makes that happen.
  • Desktop and mobile are saved separately. Changing one does not change the other unless you check Apply to Mobile and Desktop.
  • Discard Changes deletes your code. It cannot be undone.

PAGES.TITLE: Building a Custom Kendo Theme
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How the Kendo UI theme is chosen, why there is no theme builder in the admin, and how to put a custom Kendo theme file on the server.
PAGES.BODY:
Most blogs never need a custom Kendo theme. The built-in themes cover most colors and styles. This page explains when a custom theme is worth the effort, what the blog ships with, and how the theme you choose is loaded.

Table of Contents

  • What Kendo Does on Your Blog
  • What Ships With the Blog
  • When a Custom Theme Is Worth It
  • Building One
  • How the Theme Is Applied
  • Testing Your Choice
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

What Kendo Does on Your Blog

Kendo is the widget library behind the admin site and the buttons, windows, and dropdowns on your pages. Its theme sets the colors and shapes of those widgets. Matching the Kendo theme to your blog theme is what makes the page look like one design. A mismatch is the most common reason a blog looks unfinished.

What Ships With the Blog

Galaxie Blog ships with a set of ready-made Kendo themes. They include Bootstrap, Default, Flat, Material, Material Black, Metro, Metro Black, Nova, Silver, and Uniform, along with mobile variants of several of them. You choose one in the Kendo Theme dropdown in Theme Settings. Start there. Try two or three, and look at a post, a window, and the admin site with each, before you decide.

When a Custom Theme Is Worth It

Build a custom theme only when your brand needs colors and shapes that none of the built-in themes provide, and you are willing to maintain the result. A custom theme has to be rebuilt when Kendo changes, so the effort is ongoing. For most blogs, a built-in theme plus a few changes in the Custom Header Script is the better choice.

Building One

Kendo themes are built with the Telerik ThemeBuilder, which runs in a browser and produces a set of style files. Galaxie Blog's help text links to it. Note that the blog supports only the themes built from Kendo's LESS source, which is what the builder produces for current versions of Kendo.

Once you have the files, the blog needs them in its Kendo folders, and the Kendo Theme dropdown needs to list your new theme. The blog's own developer notes describe a build script for a custom Kendo bundle. If you go this way, test the result on a post, the admin site, and a phone before you use it.

How the Theme Is Applied

The theme you choose is saved with your blog theme. The page loads that theme's style file, and the blog's own styles read the theme's primary colors so the rest of the page matches. Switching the Kendo theme changes both the widgets and the page colors, so check both after each change.

Testing Your Choice

  1. Open a post, and check the buttons and the media player.
  2. Open the admin site, and check a grid, a window, and a dropdown.
  3. Open the site on a phone, and check the menu and the widgets.

Gotchas

  • Start with the built-in themes. A custom theme is ongoing work.
  • Only LESS-based Kendo themes are supported.
  • Switching themes changes the page colors too. Check the whole page afterward.

  • Themes and Grids, Start to Finish
  • Grids in Galaxie Blog
  • Settings and Options, Explained

PAGES.TITLE: Grids in Galaxie Blog
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Why the admin site uses sortable, filterable grids, the two grid versions, and the grids for content, logs, and moderation.
PAGES.BODY:
A grid is the table you use to manage almost everything in the admin site: posts, pages, categories, tags, users, subscribers, comments, fonts, and the logs. This page explains how grids work, why some need a Save button, and the difference between removing a post and deleting it.

Table of Contents

  • Why the Admin Site Uses Grids
  • How a Grid Works
  • Batch Mode and the Save Button
  • Releasing a Post From the Grid
  • Removing Versus Deleting
  • Why Logs and Search Queries Are Read-Only
  • Working With Grids Efficiently
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Why the Admin Site Uses Grids

Managing many posts one screen at a time would be slow. A grid shows a list you can sort and search, and lets you act on several rows. Once you know one grid, the others follow the same pattern, which is why the admin site feels consistent.

How a Grid Works

Each row is one item, such as a post. The columns show its details, and the buttons on the toolbar create, edit, or remove rows. Click a column heading to sort. Use the search box to narrow the list. Pages of results appear at the bottom.

Batch Mode and the Save Button

Some grids, including posts and pages, work in batch mode. In batch mode, changes you make to several rows are held until you click Save on the toolbar. This lets you change many rows in one go, but it also means a change is not final until you save. If a change does not appear, check whether you saved.

Other grids, such as fonts and themes, edit one row at a time, so each change is saved as you make it.

Releasing a Post From the Grid

The posts grid has a Released checkbox. Check it on the rows you want to release, then click Save. The grid's help text says the same thing. Check the grid's help text for the exact steps.

Removing Versus Deleting

Removing a post from the grid hides it. The post stays in the database, with a flag that marks it removed, so it no longer shows on the site. Removing is the safe choice, and it is the one the grid's remove button performs.

Deleting a post is permanent. It removes the post and its related records, such as its reads, ratings, and tags. Deleting is done from the post itself, not from the grid's remove button, and it cannot be undone. Use it only when you are sure. Before a permanent delete, make a database backup.

Why Logs and Search Queries Are Read-Only

The logs and the search queries are read-only grids. You can sort and search them, but you cannot change their rows. That is intentional, because a log is a record of what happened.

Working With Grids Efficiently

  • Sort by the date column to find recent items quickly.
  • Use the search box for a title or an alias, rather than scrolling.
  • Save after each batch of changes, so you do not lose work.

Gotchas

  • Batch changes are not saved until you click Save. Check before you leave the screen.
  • Removing hides a post. Deleting destroys it. Use remove unless you are certain.
  • Logs and search queries are read-only, by design.

See Also

  • Themes and Grids, Start to Finish
  • Comments and Moderation
  • Visitor Tracking and Banning in Galaxie Blog

PAGES.TITLE: The Theme Settings and Fonts
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The Theme Settings panels, from the custom header script to the footer, and how fonts are chosen and uploaded.
PAGES.BODY:
Theme Settings controls the look of the whole blog, and the Font Interface controls the typefaces it uses. This page explains how the screen is organized, why the panels are in the order they are, and how fonts are stored and loaded.

How Theme Settings Is Grouped

Theme Settings has many choices, and most people change only a few of them. Grouping them into panels keeps the screen manageable: you open the panel that matches the change you have in mind, and the rest stay closed. The panels are an accordion, so opening one closes the others.

The Panels, In Order

  1. Custom Header Script adds your own HTML between the page's head tags, for scripts such as analytics or verification tags.
  2. Fav Icon sets the small icon in the browser tab.
  3. Fonts chooses the typefaces for the title, the menu, and the body.
  4. Blog Theme Style and Column Display sets the Kendo theme, the dark option, and the widths of the main column and the sidebar.
  5. Backgrounds sets the page background.
  6. Header, Logo, and Blog Title control the top of every page.
  7. Menu controls the navigation bar.
  8. About & Bio Window Content sets the text of the about and bio windows.
  9. Pod Content controls the sidebar pods. See Pods, Calendar, and Archive.
  10. Footer and Custom Footer Scripts control the bottom of every page.

The order follows the top of the page to the bottom, so you can work down the screen the way a reader sees the page.

The Custom Header Script

The Custom Header Script is the most flexible panel. The text you enter is placed between the page's head tags, after the blog's own styles. Use it for scripts that must load early, such as verification tags for search engines, or for a small style rule that changes one detail without touching the theme. Keep it short and well tested, because a mistake here affects every page.

The Kendo Theme

The Kendo theme draws the widgets: buttons, windows, dropdowns, and the media player. It is chosen with the Kendo Theme dropdown, which sits in the top section of Theme Settings, above the accordion. Pick the theme whose colors match your blog. A mismatch makes buttons and the page look as though they were designed separately. See Building a Custom Kendo Theme.

Fonts Are Stored in the Blog

A font file on the server is not enough by itself. The blog keeps a record for each font: its name, its weight, whether it is italic, its file name, and whether it is a Google font. Those records let the blog choose which fonts to load. A page loads only the fonts its theme uses, which keeps pages light.

The Font Interface lists every font in that record. The grid is where you turn a font on or off, and where you can see its details.

Adding a Font

The font uploader accepts WOFF2 and WOFF files. Upload one, then check the weight, the style, and the name the uploader suggests. The uploader guesses the weight from the file name, such as 700 for bold, so confirm it. Each file can be up to 2 megabytes.

TrueType and OpenType files, with the extensions .ttf and .otf, are not accepted by the uploader. To use one, place the file in the blog's fonts folder yourself and add its style rule to the font template. Convert it to WOFF2 first if you can, since that is smaller and loads faster.

The Google Font Flag

Each font has a Is this a Google Font? checkbox, which is checked by default. In this version, the blog does not load fonts from Google's servers, so even a font marked as a Google font needs its file on your server. Leave the flag as it is unless you know a future release uses it.

A Good Order for Font Choices

  1. Choose the body font first, since it carries the most text.
  2. Choose the title font to match it, usually one with a clear personality.
  3. Choose the menu font, which should be the easiest to read at small sizes.

Gotchas

  • Only WOFF2 and WOFF upload through the screen. TrueType and OpenType need a manual copy.
  • The weight guess can be wrong. Check it before saving.
  • A Google font still needs its file on your server.

  • Building a Custom Kendo Theme
  • Grids in Galaxie Blog
  • Settings and Options, Explained

PAGES.TITLE: Themes and Grids, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The overview for making Galaxie Blog look like your site: themes, fonts, the Kendo theme underneath, and the grids you manage everything with.
PAGES.BODY:
This is the complete guide to how Galaxie Blog looks and how you manage what appears on it. A few things shape the look: the Galaxie Blog theme, the fonts it uses, the Kendo UI theme that draws the widgets underneath, and the grids you use to manage almost everything in the admin site.

Table of Contents

  • How Theme, Kendo, and Fonts Work Together
  • Start With a Built-In Theme
    • How to Pick One
  • Theme Settings
  • Fonts
    • Why the Blog Keeps a List of Fonts
    • How to Add Your Own Font
  • The Kendo Theme
  • Grids Run the Admin Site
  • A Good Order for Making a Theme
  • Troubleshooting a Theme
  • Gotchas
  • Built With
  • See Also

How Theme, Kendo, and Fonts Work Together

A page on Galaxie Blog is built in layers, and each layer can be changed separately. The Galaxie Blog theme controls the layout, colors, and typography of your pages. The Kendo UI theme controls the widgets underneath, such as buttons, windows, calendars, and dropdowns. Fonts are shared between the two. Keeping the layers separate means you can change your site's colors without rebuilding the widgets, and the reverse.

The two layers still need to agree. If your Galaxie Blog theme is dark and your Kendo theme is light, the buttons and the page will fight each other. That is why changing one often means checking the other.

Start With a Built-In Theme

Building a theme from nothing takes a long time. It is faster to start from one of the built-in themes that ship with Galaxie Blog, pick the one closest to what you want, and adjust it.

How to Pick One

  1. Open Themes & Content from the admin home screen.
  2. Look at the list of themes. Each one shows its name and whether it is the one in use.
  3. Open the theme you want and check its settings. Make your first changes there, one at a time, so you can see what each one does.

Changes in Theme Settings are previewed as you make them. Save when you are happy, and keep a note of the original values so you can go back.

Theme Settings

Theme Settings holds the look of the blog, split into panels. In order, they are: Custom Header Script, Fav Icon, Fonts, Blog Theme Style and Column Display, Backgrounds, Header, Logo, Blog Title, Menu, About and Bio Window Content, Pod Content, Footer, and Custom Footer Scripts.

The Custom Header Script panel is worth knowing about early. It lets you add your own style rules, which load after the theme's own CSS. A small rule there can override one color or one spacing value without touching the theme's files. This is the first thing to try before you replace anything.

Blog Theme Style and Column Display controls the Kendo theme, a dark option, and the widths of the main column and the sidebar. The Pod Content panel decides which sidebar pods appear. See Pods, Calendar, and Archive.

Fonts

The font list holds a set of open-source fonts that ship with the blog. You do not need to upload anything to use them. Assign a font to the title, the menu, or the body text in the Fonts panel of Theme Settings.

Why the Blog Keeps a List of Fonts

A font file on the server is not enough on its own. The blog needs to know which fonts exist, which weights and styles they come in, and which pages use them, so it only loads the fonts that are needed. A font loads on a page only when a theme uses it, which keeps pages light.

How to Add Your Own Font

Click Create New Font. Enter the weight, the type (such as sans-serif), whether it is italic, and whether it is a Google font. Font files live in /common/fonts/, so a font added by hand needs its file placed there.

Even a font marked as a Google font needs its files on your server.

The Kendo Theme

The Kendo theme draws the widgets: buttons, windows, calendars, dropdowns, and the media player. You choose one in Theme Settings, under the Kendo Theme dropdown. Galaxie Blog ships with several Kendo Core themes, and the dropdown lists the ones available in your install.

Pick a Kendo theme that matches your blog theme's colors. A mismatch is the most common reason a blog looks off. After you switch themes, check a post, a window, and the admin site, since they all use the widgets.

For a full custom Kendo theme, see Building a Custom Kendo Theme. Most sites never need one.

Grids Run the Admin Site

Almost everything you manage in the admin site is a grid, a sortable and searchable table with buttons to create, edit, and remove rows. Posts, pages, categories, tags, users, subscribers, comments, and the logs all use grids. Once you learn one, the others work the same way. See Grids in Galaxie Blog.

A Good Order for Making a Theme

  1. Choose a built-in theme close to your taste.
  2. Set the logo, the blog title, and the favicon.
  3. Pick the fonts for the title, the menu, and the body.
  4. Choose the Kendo theme that matches your colors.
  5. Set the header, the menu, and the footer.
  6. Choose the sidebar pods, and check the sidebar on a phone.
  7. Use the Custom Header Script for the last small adjustments.

Working in this order means each change sits on a stable base. If you change the colors first and then the fonts, you may have to recheck every color.

Troubleshooting a Theme

If a change does not appear on the site, the cache is the usual cause. Reload the page, then use Refresh Site in the admin. For active theme work, turn on Disable Cache in Blog Options so each change shows right away, and turn it off again afterward. See Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs.

Gotchas

  • Switching themes can change the Kendo theme. Check Blog Theme Style after every switch.
  • Only .woff2 and .woff upload directly. Other formats need a manual copy and a CSS entry.
  • Start from a built-in theme. A theme built from scratch takes much longer and is harder to keep consistent.

Built With

The widgets in the admin site and on your pages come from Kendo UI Core, the free, open-source bundle of Kendo UI for jQuery. You may use it commercially. See Software and Licenses.

  • Settings and Options, Explained

PAGES.TITLE: Visitor Tracking and Banning in Galaxie Blog
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How Galaxie Blog recognizes visitors, what the visitor log shows, and how to ban an address or a browser.
PAGES.BODY:
Galaxie Blog can record who visits your site, and it can block visitors you do not want. This page explains what is recorded, why, and how a ban works from the admin site.

What Visitor Tracking Is For

Knowing where readers come from and what they read helps you decide what to write next. Tracking is also how you spot unwanted traffic, such as a scraper that requests hundreds of pages in a minute. The visitor screens give you that view.

Turning Tracking On

Visitor logging is controlled by Enable Visitor Logging on the Blog Options screen. Turn it off on a test site if you do not want local traffic recorded. A second setting, Months to retain visitor logs, controls how long the records are kept.

What Is Recorded

For each visitor, the blog records an anonymous visitor entry with the IP address, the browser's user agent string, and the screen size. A cookie identifies returning visitors, and the cookie does not expire. Each page view is logged against that visitor. Tracking runs on the public article and page views, not on the admin site.

The Visitor Log

The Visitor Log screen lists the logged views. Open a visitor to see the Visitor Details screen, which shows the IP address, the user agent, and the signed-in user, if there is one. A visitor who is signed in as a member shows with their picture and name, in the Visitor Log's Signed in as column and at the top of their Visitor Details; click it to open them in Members. Member sign-ins have their own log, the Member Log. From there you can open that visitor's view log, or their error log.

Banning

A ban blocks a visitor by IP address, by user agent, or both. On the Visitor Details screen, check Ban IP Address?, Ban User Agent?, or both, and save. The Ban Visitors screen lets you ban and unban in bulk, and Banned Users lists every current ban.

A banned visitor receives a 403 response with the message that they have been blocked. The block applies to every page that runs the tracking check, so it covers the whole public site.

Automatic Blocking

Two things block visitors without your input. First, a list of known bad bots and scrapers is matched against each user agent, and a match creates a ban with a note saying it was automatic. Second, if one address causes five database lock errors within a minute, the blog blocks that address for fifteen minutes and returns a 429 response. Both thresholds are set in the application, not the admin site.

When an IP Ban Blocks the Wrong Reader

An IP address can be shared by many people, such as a mobile network or a school. Banning by IP can block readers who did nothing wrong. Prefer the user agent ban for a specific bot, and unban an address if you find it was a mistake.

Gotchas

  • A ban by IP can catch innocent readers who share an address.
  • Automatic bot bans are recorded as bans. Check the Banned Users list if a reader is blocked unexpectedly.
  • Turn tracking off on a test site if you do not want local traffic in your logs.

See Also

  • Comments and Moderation
  • Taming a New Galaxie Blog's Error Log: Bots, Errors and Auto-Blocking
  • Troubleshooting: Reinitialize, Restarts, and Logs

PAGES.TITLE: Comments and Moderation
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How readers leave comments, how to approve or remove them, when moderation applies, and how to handle spam.
PAGES.BODY:
Comments turn a post into a conversation. Moderation decides which comments appear right away and which wait for your review. This page explains why the defaults are set the way they are, and how to manage comments once they arrive.

What Comment Moderation Protects You From

Open comments invite good discussion, and they also invite spam and abuse. Moderation lets you keep the conversation while holding back what you do not want public. A comment from someone who is not signed in can wait for approval, which is the most common setup for a public blog.

Turning Comments On for a Post

Each post has an Allow Comments checkbox in the post editor. Turn it off to close comments on a single post. Turning it off does not remove comments already on the post.

Table of Contents

  • What Comment Moderation Protects You From
  • Turning Comments On for a Post
  • Reviewing Comments
  • What Waits for Approval
  • Handling Spam
  • A Routine
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Reviewing Comments

Each comment opens in a detail window showing the post it belongs to, the date it was posted, the commenter, and two checkboxes: Approved and Moderated. Approve a comment to show it on the post. Mark it moderated once you have reviewed it, so you can tell which comments you have already looked at.

When a comment is approved, the people who subscribed to that post's comments receive a notice. The subscribe option appears on the comment form.

What Waits for Approval

When moderation is on, a comment from someone who is not signed in is held until you approve it. A signed-in user's comment is handled according to the blog's settings. Because the blog-wide moderation setting is read by the server, check it on your own site before you rely on it.

Handling Spam

Leave unapproved spam unapproved, and remove it. Repeat offenders can be banned by IP address from the visitor screens, which is described in Visitor Tracking and Banning in Galaxie Blog. A ban is stronger than a single removal, because it stops the same person from posting again.

A Routine

  1. Check the held comments once or twice a week.
  2. Approve the real ones, and mark them moderated.
  3. Remove the spam, and ban a source that keeps coming back.

Gotchas

  • Turning off Allow Comments does not hide existing comments. They stay on the post.
  • Approving a comment notifies subscribers. Approve only comments you intend to publish.

See Also

  • Subscribers and Email Notifications
  • Scheduling a Post

PAGES.TITLE: Reactions and the Reaction Log
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How readers like or dislike a post, and how to review those reactions in the Reaction Log.
PAGES.BODY:
Readers can react to a post with a like or a dislike. This page explains how the reactions work for readers, what the Reaction Log shows you, and how to use the log to decide what to write or fix next.

Table of Contents

  • What Are Reactions?
  • What Readers See
  • The One-Vote Rule
  • The Reaction Log
  • Removing a Vote
  • A Worked Example
  • Using Reactions Well
  • Gotchas

What Are Reactions?

Comments take effort, so most readers never leave one. Likes and dislikes are a quick way for a reader to say a post helped, or did not. For you, they are a signal that costs nothing to collect. A post that many readers dislike may need a clearer title, a better intro, or a correction. The Reaction Log lets you see those signals by post and by date, so you can decide what to fix, instead of guessing from comments alone.

What Readers See

Under each post, readers see two buttons: Like this post and Dislike this post. A reader clicks one, and the vote is saved right away. No page reload is needed, and the reader does not need an account.

The One-Vote Rule

Each visitor gets one vote per post. If a visitor tries to vote again on the same post, the blog refuses the second vote, because the first one is already saved. A vote cannot be switched from like to dislike.

The blog recognizes a visitor with a browser cookie. A visitor who clears their cookies, uses a private window, or switches browsers counts as a new visitor and can vote again. For that reason, the counts show interest, not an exact number of readers.

The Reaction Log

Open Reaction Log from the admin site. Each row is one vote, with these columns:

Column What it shows
UserId The anonymous user id that voted. It links the vote to a visitor record.
IP Address The address the vote came from.
Post The post the vote was made on.
User Agent The visitor's browser.
Like Set when the vote was a like.
Dislike Set when the vote was a dislike.
Date When the vote was made.

All columns can be sorted, and most can be searched. To search, type the term at the top of a column, then click the search link at the right of the page. Sort by Post to see every vote on one post, or by Date to see recent activity.

Removing a Vote

To remove a vote, click the edit icon on its row, select the vote you want to remove, and then click the update checkmark on the right of the page. The vote is removed, and that visitor can vote on the post again.

A Worked Example

Say a post on your blog has far more dislikes than likes. Follow these steps:

  1. Open the Reaction Log and sort by Post, so all the votes for each post sit together.
  2. Find the post and count its likes and dislikes. Look at the Date column to see whether the dislikes came all at once.
  3. Check the IP Address and User Agent columns. If many dislikes come from one address, or from automated browsers, treat them with caution. See Visitor Tracking and Banning in Galaxie Blog.
  4. If the dislikes look genuine, reread the post. Common causes are a misleading title, an intro that does not say what the post covers, or an error in the steps.

Using Reactions Well

  • Read patterns, not single votes. A few dislikes from one reader tell you little.
  • Compare posts with each other. A post with many dislikes next to posts with mostly likes is worth a closer look.
  • Reactions do not change what readers see. They do not hide or reorder posts. Use them as feedback for editing.

Gotchas

  • Cookies decide who has voted. Repeat voters who clear cookies can vote again.
  • The log is a list of votes. It does not show the reader's comment, so read the post's comments too when you are trying to understand a dislike.

PAGES.TITLE: Search Queries
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What visitors search for on your blog, and how to review the Search Queries log in the admin site.
PAGES.BODY:
The Search Queries screen shows what visitors typed into your site's search box. It is a window into what readers are looking for, which is often different from what you think they want. This page explains what is recorded and how to use it.

Table of Contents

  • What Readers' Searches Tell You
  • What Is Recorded
  • Reading the Screen
  • How to Use the Results
  • Privacy Notes
  • Gotchas

What Readers' Searches Tell You

A search that finds nothing is a reader telling you what they wanted. If the same term appears again and again without a matching post, that is a gap in your writing. If a common term matches a post that does not answer it, that post may need a better title or description. The queries are free research, and they come straight from your readers.

What Is Recorded

Each search records the text the visitor typed, the date, and the visitor it came from. The visitor record gives the IP address, the user agent, and the signed-in user, if there is one. The screen is read-only, so you can review the queries without changing them.

Reading the Screen

The Search Queries screen lists each search with its date, the user, the IP address, the user agent, and the search terms. The list is sorted with the newest search first. Scan the Search Terms column for a term you care about.

How to Use the Results

  1. Look for terms that appear several times. A repeated term is a real interest.
  2. Search your site for the same term. If nothing matches, write a post about it.
  3. If a post matches but readers still search for the term, check that the post's title and description use the words readers use.

Privacy Notes

Search queries can contain anything a visitor types, including names or personal details. Treat the list as private. Do not publish it, and do not share the raw list outside your team. If you need to show trends, summarize them first.

Gotchas

  • The list shows every search, including typos. Look for patterns rather than single entries.
  • A search can contain personal information. Keep the list private.
  • The screen is read-only. You cannot edit or clear a search from it.

PAGES.TITLE: Taming a New Galaxie Blogs Error Log: Bots, Errors and Auto-Blocking
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Why a new blog fills its error log with requests for files it does not have, how to tell those bot errors from real problems, and what to block.
PAGES.BODY:
The error log records problems on your site. Left alone, it fills with noise from bots and repeated mistakes. This page explains where errors are recorded, how to read the Error Log, and how the blog deals with bursts of errors on its own.

Table of Contents

  • Where Errors Are Saved
  • The Error Log Screen
  • Bots and Scrapers
  • Automatic Throttling
  • Error Emails: A Nightly Summary
  • A Routine for Keeping the Log Useful
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Where Errors Are Saved

Errors are saved to the database, where you can read them in the admin site. They are also written to a log file on the server. The database copy is for daily use, and the file copy is the backup you can read if the admin site itself is broken.

The Error Log Screen

The Error Log groups errors by IP address. Each row shows the error ID, the error message, the IP address, how many times it happened, whether it is resolved, and whether it looks like a bot. Open a row to see the details. The retention setting, Retain error and administrative logs for, controls how long these records are kept.

Grouping by IP helps you tell a single broken page from a flood of requests from one source. A high count from one address usually means a bot, not a bug in your code.

Bots and Scrapers

Some automated visitors are not interested in your content. They request pages in bulk, probe for software weaknesses, or collect text for other services. The blog keeps a list of known bad bots and scrapers, covering AI training crawlers, SEO crawlers, and security scanners. A visitor whose user agent matches the list is banned automatically, with a note that says so.

Good bots, such as search engine crawlers, are not on that list, so they are not blocked.

Automatic Throttling

When the database is under pressure, errors can pile up quickly. The blog watches for that. If one IP address causes five database lock errors within sixty seconds, the blog blocks that address for fifteen minutes. A blocked visitor gets a 429 response, meaning too many requests, and their errors are not logged again during the block. This stops one aggressive client from making the whole site slower for everyone else.

Error Emails: A Nightly Summary

With Send Diagnostics on, the blog emails you about errors. By default it sends one summary a night instead of an email for every new error, so a bad day doesn't bury your inbox. The summary lists every error since the last one:

  • new errors first, marked NEW, then the most frequent;
  • for each one, the message, the file and line, an example address, how many times it happened since the last summary, and when it last happened;
  • errors that look like bots probing for pages and files that don't exist, collapsed into one line at the end;
  • a link to the Error Log, which still has every detail, including the stack traces.

Nothing is sent on a night without errors. If many errors happen at once (100 or more within ten minutes, which can mean the site is down), you still get one email right away, and at most one every six hours after that.

Choose how errors are emailed in Blog Options, under Error emails: A nightly summary (the default) or Right away, for each new error. Send it after sets the time, in the blog's time zone (2 AM by default), and Send a summary now sends one for the last 24 hours straight away. The summary is sent by the first page view after that time, not by a scheduled task, so it also works on servers where scheduled tasks can't call the blog.

A Routine for Keeping the Log Useful

  1. Open the Error Log once a week and sort by count.
  2. For each high-count row, check whether it is a bot. If it is, the automatic ban may already cover it.
  3. For each real error, fix the cause, then mark the row resolved so you can see what is still open.

Gotchas

  • A high count from one IP is usually a bot. Check before you hunt for a code bug.
  • Throttled addresses are not logged while they are blocked, so a quiet log does not always mean a healthy site.
  • Automatic bans can be wrong. Check Banned Users if a real reader is blocked.
  • The first summary comes right away. After upgrading, the first page view sends a summary of the last 24 hours. After that, it comes once a night.

PAGES.TITLE: Subscribers and Email Notifications
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How readers subscribe to a post, how they confirm, what gets emailed, and how they unsubscribe.
PAGES.BODY:
Subscribers are readers who asked to hear about new posts. This page explains how people subscribe, why each subscription must be confirmed, how you manage the list, and what gets sent when you release a post.

Table of Contents

  • Why Subscribers Must Confirm
  • How People Subscribe
  • Adding a Subscriber Yourself
  • The Subscriber List
  • What Gets Sent on Release
  • Comment Notices
  • Keeping the List Healthy
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Why Subscribers Must Confirm

Anyone can type any address into a form. Confirmation makes sure the address belongs to the person asking, and it keeps the list clean. An address that never confirms is not a subscriber, so it never receives your posts. The blog removes unconfirmed addresses on its own after a time, which keeps the list from filling with mistyped or fake entries.

How People Subscribe

A reader enters an address in the subscribe form. The blog records the address with a verification token and sends a confirmation email. The reader must follow the link in that email to become a verified subscriber. Until then, the address stays unverified.

A form can also offer "Email me new posts" at the end. Someone who ticks it gets the same confirmation email, and becomes a subscriber after confirming. Subscribers are also listed in Members, marked "not confirmed" until they confirm.

Adding a Subscriber Yourself

You can add a subscriber from the admin site with the Add Subscriber screen. Use this for a reader who asked you by another route, such as a conversation or a form. Make sure the address is one that person actually uses.

The Subscriber List

The subscriber grid lists every subscriber and whether they have been verified. Use it to check your count, to find an address you want to remove, and to spot entries that never confirmed. Removing a subscriber stops all future mail to that address.

What Gets Sent on Release

When you save a released blog post in the post editor, the blog asks whether to email subscribers. If you say yes, every verified subscriber receives the post, and the post is marked as emailed. If it was already emailed, the prompt asks whether to send it again. Say yes and it is sent again, so subscribers receive it a second time.

A post scheduled for a later time is emailed automatically when it goes live. Releasing a post from the Blog Posts grid works a little differently: there, the prompt only appears for a post that has never been emailed. Pages are never emailed.

The email holds the post itself. If the post has a table of contents, it is left out of the email, because its links only work on the page.

Comment Notices

Subscribers to a single post's comments are a separate list. They get a notice when a comment on that post is approved. This is controlled by the subscribe option on the comment form, not by the main subscriber list.

Keeping the List Healthy

  • Review the list now and then, and remove addresses that bounce.
  • Never buy or import addresses. Subscribers should always ask to hear from you.
  • Keep the mail settings correct, as described in Email and Comments.

Gotchas

  • An unconfirmed address does not receive post emails.
  • A scheduled post is emailed automatically when it goes live. Check the prompt after the post goes live.
  • Saying yes to the email prompt always sends, even if the post was emailed before.

PAGES.TITLE: Scheduling a Post
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to schedule a post to release itself at a future date and time, and how to reschedule or cancel it.
PAGES.BODY:
Scheduling lets you write a post now and have it go live at a time you choose. This page explains why scheduling is useful, how the release time is stored, and what to check before you rely on it.

Table of Contents

  • Scheduling Versus Publishing Now
  • Scheduling a Post
  • What Happens When You Schedule
  • Cancelling
  • Checking the Status
  • Emails for Scheduled Posts
  • A Good Habit
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Scheduling Versus Publishing Now

Readers often look for new posts at particular times, and you may not be at your computer then. Scheduling lets you finish a post when it is ready and publish it when it will reach the most readers. It also lets you prepare a series of posts and release them one at a time.

Scheduling a Post

Open the post, and choose the Schedule Release option in the Misc section. The window has a date and time picker labeled Release Date & Time. Choose the time, then click Schedule. If the post is already scheduled, the button reads Reschedule.

The time must be in the future. The window refuses a time that has already passed.

What Happens When You Schedule

The blog keeps the post unreleased until the time you chose. It also creates a one-time task on the server that runs at that time, which releases the post. The task is replaced if you reschedule, so only one release is pending at a time. The time you enter is converted from your blog's time zone to the server's time zone, so the release happens at the time you meant.

Cancelling

Click Cancel Scheduled Release to remove the pending task. Cancelling leaves the post in its current state, so if you want it live, check the Released box yourself.

Checking the Status

The window shows whether a release is pending and when it is due. Check it after you schedule, to confirm the time is right.

Emails for Scheduled Posts

A scheduled post does not email your subscribers on its own. When you release a post by hand, the blog asks whether to send the email. A scheduled release goes live without that prompt, so check the post once it is live and send the email yourself if you want subscribers to hear about it. See Subscribers and Email Notifications.

A Good Habit

  • Preview the post before you schedule it, so the release is not the first time you see it.
  • Check the time zone on the window, since it matters for the release.
  • Check the post after it goes live, to confirm it looks right and to send any email.

Gotchas

  • A scheduled post does not email subscribers. Send the email yourself after it goes live.
  • Cancelling does not publish the post. It only removes the pending release.
  • The time must be in the future. A past time is refused.

PAGES.TITLE: Categories, Tags, and Related Posts
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Organizing posts with categories and tags, and how related posts are chosen.
PAGES.BODY:
Categories, tags, and related posts are how readers move between your posts. Categories give the blog a broad structure, tags add detail, and related posts suggest what to read next. This page explains the purpose of each, and how to use them without clutter.

Table of Contents

  • Categories, Tags, and Related Posts
  • Categories
  • Tags
  • Related Posts
  • Breadcrumbs
  • How to Keep It Tidy
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Categories, Tags, and Related Posts

Each one answers a different reader question. A category answers "what is this blog about, broadly?" A tag answers "what specific topics does this post touch?" A related post answers "what else should I read about this?" Using all three gives a reader several ways in, without forcing them through one menu.

Categories

A category is a broad group, such as Tutorials or News. Each post can belong to a category, and the category archive lists every post in it. Create a category from the category screen, or from the editor when you need one that does not exist yet.

A category needs a unique name and a unique alias. The alias becomes the part of the address that identifies the category. It cannot contain spaces, commas, question marks, or ampersands, because those characters break addresses. Choose a short alias you will not need to change.

Tags

Tags are finer. Use them for the specific subjects in a post, such as a tool name or a technique. A post can have several tags. Tags are chosen in the post editor's Tags box, and you can create one there as you type. Keep tags consistent. Use the same spelling each time, so one topic does not split into several tags.

Related Posts

Related posts are chosen by hand in the editor's Related Posts box, which shows Select Related Post... as its placeholder. The link works both ways, so choosing a related post also links that post back to yours. The full logic is described in Popular Posts and Related Blogs.

Breadcrumbs

Categories appear in the breadcrumb trail. A post shows its categories after Home, and a category archive shows Home, then Blog, then the category name. Page collections use the same kind of trail, described on the Page Collections page.

How to Keep It Tidy

  • Keep a short list of categories. Five to ten is plenty for most blogs.
  • Give each post two or three tags, not ten.
  • Choose two or three related posts that a reader would genuinely want next.

Gotchas

  • Aliases cannot contain spaces, commas, question marks, or ampersands. The screen rejects them.
  • Similar tags split a topic. Pick one spelling and keep it.
  • Related posts are manual. A new post does not join other posts' lists until you add it.

PAGES.TITLE: Post Editing, Start to Finish
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: The whole post workflow in one place: writing, dating, releasing, and organizing a post.
PAGES.BODY:
This is the complete guide to writing a post, from the first title to the moment it goes live. It covers the editor, the order most people work in, and the reasons behind each step.

Table of Contents

  • How the Post Editor Is Built
  • Step 1: Set the Title and the Date
  • Step 2: Write the Body
  • Step 3: Add the Main Picture
  • Step 4: Describe the Post
  • Step 5: Check the Buttons and the Misc Section
  • Step 6: Preview, Then Release
  • Working Habits That Save Time
  • Gotchas
  • Built With
  • See Also

How the Post Editor Is Built

Galaxie Blog's post editor is a rich text editor, so you see the result as you write. It is a customized version of TinyMCE, which is free, open-source software. The blog has tools for most of what a post needs, so you do not have to paste in code for everyday formatting. The settings that decide who sees a post and when sit in their own section, so the writing stays uncluttered.

Step 1: Set the Title and the Date

Start at the top of the editor. The title is the headline, and it also starts the post's address. The Date Posted is a date and time picker. A post drafted over several days should use the date it goes live, so it does not look old in your feed. See Dates and Sort Order.

Step 2: Write the Body

Write in the body editor. It has the usual tools: paragraph styles, bold and italic, alignment, lists, indentation, links, anchors, special characters, and tables. Text pasted from Word, Google Docs, or Excel is cleaned up as it goes in.

For headings, use the heading tools rather than bold text. Headings give the post its structure, and they are what the table of contents reads. See Formatting Post Content.

The Insert menu adds the rest: images, media, galleries, carousels, custom windows, maps, templates, and code samples. Each of those has its own page in this section.

Step 3: Add the Main Picture

Open the Enclosure Editor to set the picture, video, map, or carousel that opens the post. It is also the picture on the card and in social shares, so it is worth taking a moment over. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

Step 4: Describe the Post

The Description is a short summary of the post, up to 1,250 characters. The blog uses it on cards, in previews, and in search results. Write it as a sentence a reader would want to read, not as a copy of the first paragraph.

Then add a category and tags. Categories give the post a broad place in the blog, and tags add the detail. Related posts can be chosen by hand. See Categories, Tags, and Related Posts.

Step 5: Check the Buttons and the Misc Section

The buttons row opens the windows for the less common parts of a post. Alias changes the address. Post Header holds the optional directives. CSS and JavaScript let you style or script one post. The Misc section holds the release settings: Preview, Set Theme, Schedule Release, JSON-LD, Released, Allow Comments, Promote, and Remove. See The Edit Post Interface, Updated for each one.

Step 6: Preview, Then Release

Click Preview to see the post as a reader will. Check the picture, the headings, and the card. Then check Released and click Submit. The blog asks whether to set the date to today and whether to email subscribers. See Releasing, Promoting, and Removing a Post.

Working Habits That Save Time

  • Save a draft early. Nothing is public until the post is released, so drafts are safe.
  • Write the title and the Description last. By the time you finish the body, you know what the post says.
  • Preview on a phone. The post looks different on a small screen, and most readers use one.

Gotchas

  • The Description is capped at 1,250 characters. A longer one is cut off on cards.
  • A post stays hidden while a schedule is pending. Released only checks at the release moment. See Scheduling a Post.
  • Maps need an Azure Maps key. Without it, map features do not work.

Built With

The post editor is TinyMCE 5.5.1, licensed under the LGPL 2.1. Commercial use is allowed, and changes to TinyMCE's own files must be shared under the same license. Code samples are highlighted with Prism, which is MIT licensed. Maps use Azure Maps, a paid Microsoft service you connect with your own key. See Software and Licenses.

PAGES.TITLE: The Edit Post Interface, Updated
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: A field-by-field tour of the post editor: the top fields, CSS and Scripts, Misc, the body editor, and the description.
PAGES.BODY:
The post editor is the screen where you write a post and set everything about it. It is a rich text editor for the body, with a separate editor for the main picture, and a set of settings for when and how the post appears. This page walks through each part, and explains why each one is there.

Table of Contents

  • Body Editor vs Edit Post Window
  • The Body Editor
  • The Enclosure
  • The Top Fields
    • Date Posted
    • Author and Title
  • The Buttons Row
  • The Misc Section
  • Categories, Tags, and Related Posts
  • Good to Know
  • See Also

Body Editor vs Edit Post Window

The body of a post is text, so it uses a rich text editor that shows you the result as you type. The main picture, video, or map is a different kind of content, with its own upload and crop steps. Keeping them in separate editors means a large video or a crop does not get in the way of your writing, and you can change the hero without touching the text.

The Body Editor

The body editor is a customized version of TinyMCE, which is free, open-source software released under the MIT license. Galaxie Blog uses it without limits or upcharges.

It handles the usual writing tools: undo and redo, paragraph styles, bold and italic, alignment, bullets, indentation, links and anchors, special characters, and HTML tables. Text you paste from Word, Google Docs, or Excel is cleaned up, so the formatting from those programs does not carry over.

The Insert menu holds the media and the blocks: images, links, media, galleries, carousels, custom windows, maps, map directions, templates, code samples, and tables. Each one has its own page in this section, such as Adding an Image to a Post, Galleries and Carousels, and Formatting Post Content.

The Enclosure

The enclosure is the large picture, video, map, or carousel at the top of the post. It is also the picture readers see on the card, so it does a lot of work in a small space. You set it in the Enclosure Editor, which is a separate window from the body.

In the Enclosure Editor you can upload an image or a video, add a video cover and captions, make a static map, build a route with several stops, or create a carousel. When you upload an image, Galaxie Blog creates the optimized copies for Facebook, Twitter, and Google. See Enclosures: What a Post Shows First.

The Top Fields

At the top of the editor are the Date Posted, the Author, and the Title, followed by the post type, in two rows: Blog post (Article or Event) and Page (Page or Booking). An event has an Event details button in its row, and a booking page a Booking details button; see Events and Sign-Ups and Bookings and Booking Pages. Booking is only offered on pages. Pages are edited the same way as posts, but they are treated differently in feeds and email.

Date Posted

The Date Posted is a date and time picker. It can be a past date or a future one. When you release a post, the editor asks whether to change the date to today. Say no to keep the date you chose. If the date is in the future, the editor offers to schedule the release. See Scheduling a Post and Dates and Sort Order.

Author and Title

If the blog has more than one author, an administrator can change the author here. The title is the headline of the post, and it also sets the start of the post's address.

The Buttons Row

The row under the title opens the windows for the less common parts of a post:

  • Alias changes the friendly name in the address. It is saved right away. The reason it saves on its own is that an address change should not depend on the rest of the form. See Post URLs and Redirects.
  • Post Header holds the optional post directives, which set search and sharing details, attach scripts, and include templates. See Advanced: XML Post Directives and JSON-LD.
  • CSS opens a CSS editor, so you can style one post without changing the theme.
  • JavaScript opens a script editor. It is useful for setting up a widget, such as a Kendo grid, on a single post.

The Misc Section

The Misc section holds the settings that decide who sees the post and when:

  • Preview shows the post as a reader will see it, so you can check it before it goes live.
  • Set Theme gives this post its own theme. Other posts are not affected.
  • Schedule Release releases the post at a time you choose. See Scheduling a Post.
  • JSON-LD (SEO) lets you write the structured data by hand. Most of the time you do not need to, since Galaxie Blog generates it.
  • Released makes the post public. Until it is checked, only administrators can see the post.
  • Allow Comments turns comments on or off for this post.
  • Promote moves the post to the top of the main page with a highlight. It is for blog posts, not pages.
  • Remove takes the post off the blog. You can then add a redirect, or delete the post for good. See Releasing, Promoting, and Removing a Post.

Categories, Tags, and Related Posts

Below the body you assign a category and tags. Those help readers find related posts, and you can also choose related posts by hand. See Categories, Tags, and Related Posts.

Good to Know

  • Every editor previews its media, including videos and maps, so you can check the result as you go.
  • Check the size limits before a large upload. Image and video limits are set in Blog Options. For a very large video, hosting it yourself and linking to it can be easier.
  • Maps use Azure Maps. Older posts that used Bing Maps still display, but new maps need an Azure Maps key. See Maps in Posts.

PAGES.TITLE: Dates and Sort Order
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: What Date Posted does, how to schedule a post for the future, and how the sort date controls where a post appears in the list.
PAGES.BODY:
Every post has two dates that matter: the date it was posted, and the sort date that decides where it appears in the blog's list. Most of the time they are the same. This page explains why there are two, and how to change the order without changing the date a reader sees.

Table of Contents

  • Date Posted vs Post Sort Date
  • Setting the Date Posted
  • Changing the Sort Order
  • How Dates Appear
  • When to Use Each
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Date Posted vs Post Sort Date

The date posted is the true date of the post. It is what you show as the publication date, and it is what the archives use. The sort date controls the post's place in the main list. Keeping them separate lets you move a post up or down the list, for example to feature an important post, without making it look as though you wrote it on a different day.

Setting the Date Posted

The Date Posted field is a date and time picker. A new post starts with the current date and time. A draft written over several days should use the date you release it, so it does not look old in the feed. Scheduling a post sets this date automatically to the release time.

Changing the Sort Order

To move a post in the main list without changing its date, open the Post Sort Date window from the post. Choose a sort date between two other posts, and the post moves into that position. The window's help text explains this. The post's displayed date does not change.

The blog marks a post as sorted differently when its sort date and its date posted do not match, so you can tell at a glance which posts have been moved.

How Dates Appear

The date posted is what readers see on the post.

When to Use Each

  • Use the date posted for the true publication date.
  • Use the sort date to feature a post, or to put a series in order, without changing the dates readers see.
  • Use a future date only through scheduling, which handles the release for you.

Gotchas

  • A moved post keeps its date. The sort date changes the position only.
  • A future date does not publish on its own. Use the scheduling window instead.

PAGES.TITLE: Custom Windows in a Post
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How to add a popup window inside a post, with rich text or your own ColdFusion template.
PAGES.BODY:
A custom window is a panel you can open from inside a post, to hold extra content that does not belong in the flow of the text. This page explains why the feature exists, how to create one, and what to watch for.

Table of Contents

  • When to Use a Custom Window
  • Creating One
  • Placing the Button
  • Pixels vs Percentages for Window Size
  • Reusing a Window
  • A Good Use
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

When to Use a Custom Window

Some content supports a post without being part of its story: a glossary, a set of instructions, a sign-up note, or a long table a reader may want to check. Putting it inline makes the post long and hard to follow. A custom window keeps it one click away, and the reader opens it only when they need it.

Creating One

In the post editor, choose Create Custom Window from the toolbar or the Insert menu. The picker lets you create a new window or choose one you already made, so you can reuse the same window in several posts.

The editor asks for these details:

  • Button Label, the words on the button that opens the window. Required, up to 125 characters.
  • Window Title, the heading shown at the top of the window. Required, at least three characters.
  • Unit of measurement, pixels or a percentage, for the window's size.
  • Window Height and Window Width, the size of the window in the unit you chose.
  • Content, the text and formatting the window shows.
  • Cfinclude Path, an optional template to include instead of typed content. Use it when the content is built by code.
  • Active, which turns the window on or off without deleting it.

Placing the Button

After you save, the blog places a button at your cursor in the editor. You can move the button later like any other element. The success message offers a view-source option, so you can see the markup if you want to check it.

Pixels vs Percentages for Window Size

A window sized in pixels stays the same size on every screen, which can be too wide on a phone. A percentage adapts to the screen. Use pixels when you need a fixed size, and a percentage when the window should fill the space it has.

Reusing a Window

Because a window can be chosen from the picker, you can insert the same window into more than one post. Changing the window changes it everywhere it is used, so review each post after an edit. Set a window to inactive if you want to hide it without removing it from posts.

A Good Use

Use a custom window for a short, self-contained block that a reader may or may not need, such as a definition, a checklist, or a note about a tool. Keep the main story in the post, and keep the window supportive.

Gotchas

  • Check the saved size on the post after you save. If a width looks wrong, report it, since the width field has a known naming issue.
  • Inactive windows are hidden, not deleted. Turn one back on to restore it.
  • A change to a reused window affects every post that uses it.

PAGES.TITLE: Post URLs and Redirects
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How a post address is built, how to change its alias safely, and how redirects keep old links working.
PAGES.BODY:
Every post has an address, and the address is built from two parts: the date the post was created, and a short name called the alias. This page explains how that address is built, how to change the alias safely, and how a redirect keeps old links working.

Table of Contents

  • How Post Addresses Are Built
  • How the Alias Is Made
  • How to Change the Alias
  • Changing a Released Post's Title
  • How Redirects Work
  • When to Change an Address
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

How Post Addresses Are Built

A post's address is made of the post date and the alias, for example /blog/2022/5/20/introducing-the-galaxie-blog-administrative-site. The date gives the post a place in time, and the alias gives it a readable name. Search engines and readers both use the address to understand what a page is about, so a clear alias helps them.

How the Alias Is Made

When you create a post, the alias is built from the title, with spaces turned into dashes. Blog titles can be long, so you can shorten the alias without changing the title. The title and the alias are separate, and changing one does not force a change to the other.

How to Change the Alias

  1. Open the post in the editor.
  2. Click Alias in the buttons row (or Change Alias in the Misc section on a small screen).
  3. Type the new alias. Use letters, numbers, and dashes. Spaces and special characters are not allowed.
  4. Save. The alias is saved right away, and the address updates.

The alias saves on its own, separately from the rest of the form. That way a change to the address never depends on whether the rest of the post is ready.

Changing a Released Post's Title

If you change the title of a released post, the blog asks Change Title and Link?. A yes changes the alias to match the new title, and the old address stops working. A no keeps the address the same. Answer no if the post has been shared, linked, or indexed, because a changed address breaks every link that points at it.

How Redirects Work

A redirect sends visitors from an old address to a new one. When you remove a released post, the blog offers to create one. You choose Permanent (301), which tells search engines the content has moved for good, or Temporary (302), for a short-term move. Readers who follow the old link land on the new page instead of a not-found error.

A redirect belongs to the removed post, so deleting the post also deletes the redirect. If you want the redirect to stay, keep the post removed rather than deleting it.

When to Change an Address

  • A new post with a clumsy alias: change it before you share the post. There is no cost.
  • A published post you want to rename: change it only if you add a redirect for the old address.
  • A post you are moving to a new topic: remove the old one with a redirect, and create a new post.

Gotchas

  • Keep aliases short and plain. Long aliases are harder to share and read.
  • Changing a shared address breaks links. Add a redirect whenever you change one that is already public.
  • Admin-only changes are safe to test. Draft posts can change their alias freely.

PAGES.TITLE: Formatting Post Content
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Markdown shortcuts, the automatic table of contents, code samples with Prism, and galleries and carousels.
PAGES.BODY:
Formatting turns a block of text into something a reader can scan. The editor gives you the tools most writers need, and it cleans up text you paste in. This page explains the reason behind each group of tools and how to use them well.

Table of Contents

  • Formatting for Structure
  • The Toolbar
  • The Insert Menu
  • Headings and the Table of Contents
  • Code Samples
  • Pasting From Other Programs
  • Links
  • A Few Habits
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Formatting for Structure

A post with clear headings, short paragraphs, and lists is easier to read on a phone and easier for search engines to understand. The headings also build the table of contents and the outline. So the best formatting is structure, not decoration. Use headings to mark sections, bold for a word that matters, and lists for steps or options.

The Toolbar

The desktop toolbar holds undo and redo, a style menu, bold and italic, the four alignments, bulleted and numbered lists, indent and outdent, links, images, media, and the fancy gallery. On a phone, the toolbar is shorter, with the most used tools only.

The style menu sets the block style of a paragraph, such as a heading or a normal paragraph. Use it for headings rather than making text bold and large by hand. Headings are what the blog reads to build the table of contents.

The Insert Menu

The Insert menu holds the larger items: images, gradients, animations, links, media, galleries, carousels, custom windows, maps, templates, code samples, tables, special characters, emoticons, horizontal rules, page breaks, anchors, the table of contents, and the date. Each has its own page in this section.

Headings and the Table of Contents

The table of contents is built from your headings. Insert it with the Insert menu, and the blog creates a list of links to each heading, going down five levels. When you edit a heading, the blog updates the link so it still points to the right place. Give headings clear names, because the names become the link text.

Code Samples

Code samples are highlighted with Prism, so readers see color-coded code. Choose the language from the list, which includes HTML, JavaScript, CSS, C#, CFScript, Java, JSON, PHP, Python, Ruby, and SQL. Pick the right language, since it controls the colors.

Pasting From Other Programs

Text pasted from Word or a web page brings along formatting that can clash with the blog's style. The editor's paste tool strips most of it. Check the result, and remove any stray colors or fonts, so the post keeps the blog's look.

Links

Use the link tool to connect a word to a page. Link to other posts on your own site with their full addresses, and link to outside sites when a reader would benefit. Use descriptive link text rather than a bare address or the words "click here."

A Few Habits

  • Use one heading level for each section, and keep the levels in order.
  • Keep paragraphs short, a few sentences each.
  • Preview the post on a phone before you release it.

Gotchas

  • Bold text is not a heading. It will not appear in the table of contents.
  • Pasted formatting can clash with the theme. Check the result after pasting.
  • Choose the code language. The wrong one gives the wrong colors.

PAGES.TITLE: Adding an Image to a Post
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: How images are added to a post, what happens to each upload, and how to control the crop and compression.
PAGES.BODY:
Adding media to your posts is simple in Galaxie Blog. You can upload the popular image formats, such as jpg, png, gif, and webp, and you can embed video and maps too. Every picture you add is optimized for you, so it looks right on phones, on computers, and when it is shared.

Table of Contents

  • Automatic Image Optimization
  • Two Places to Add a Picture
  • The Insert Image Window
  • Picking a Good Picture
  • Editing a Picture
  • Video Is Handled Separately
  • Gotchas
  • Built With
  • See Also

Automatic Image Optimization

Readers see your pictures on phones, on laptops, and in social previews, and each of those needs a different size and shape. Making those copies by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. Galaxie Blog makes them when you upload, so every picture is ready for every place it appears, and the full-size original is never shared by accident.

Two Places to Add a Picture

You can add a picture in two places. The Enclosure Editor attaches it to the top of the post, where it is also used as the hero image and on the card. The body editor lets you place a picture inline, in the middle of your text. Either way, you can crop or rotate the picture before it is saved.

When you upload an enclosure, Galaxie Blog creates the optimized versions for Facebook, Twitter, and Google, and the thumbnails for the blog's pages. See Image Optimization and WebP for the details.

The Insert Image Window

To open it, click the image icon in the body editor, or choose Insert, Image. The window does a few things:

  • You can link to a picture by pasting its address into the source field. If the picture exists, you get a preview, and the width and height fill in for you.
  • You can write a short description of the picture. It is read by screen readers and by search engines, so describe what the picture shows.
  • You can drag a picture from your computer into the window, or browse for one. On a phone, you can also use the camera.

Picking a Good Picture

For the best results when a post is shared, use a landscape picture that is at least 1200 pixels wide and 675 pixels high. Compress large pictures before you upload them. Very large files can fail to upload, and the current limits are set in Blog Options.

Editing a Picture

Click a picture in the body and then click the edit image icon. The tools are simple sliders and icons, such as rotate left, rotate right, flip, and crop. Your changes are saved with the picture, so you do not need to edit it again later.

Video Is Handled Separately

Video and maps have their own steps, because they need more than a picture does. See Video in a Post and Maps in Posts. Galaxie Blog also includes galleries and carousels, which are covered in Galleries and Carousels.

Gotchas

  • Only the image formats the blog accepts will upload. If a file is rejected, convert it to jpg, png, gif, or webp.
  • Describe every picture. A description helps the people and the search engines that cannot see it.

Built With

Uploads use Uppy, which is MIT licensed, and the cropping tool is part of that upload window. See Software and Licenses.
