PAGES.TITLE: Advanced: XML Post Directives and JSON-LD
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Post directives that change how a post is shared and described to search engines, the custom include directive, the more tag, and the generated JSON-LD.
PAGES.BODY:
Most of what a post needs is set in the editor. For a few advanced jobs, the blog reads special directives you add to a post's header, and it can produce structured data for search engines. This page explains what those are, why they exist, and when you should and should not use them.

Table of Contents

  • When You Need Directives
  • How a Directive Is Written
  • The Video Directives
  • The Search and Social Directives
  • JSON-LD
  • When to Use These
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

When You Need Directives

The editor covers the common cases, but some settings are rare enough that a screen would be cluttered by them. Directives let you set those few settings by writing a short tag in the post's header field. They are a shortcut for experienced users, and they are not needed for an ordinary post.

How a Directive Is Written

A directive is a short tag with a name and a value, placed in the post header field. The blog reads the name, and it uses the value in place of the default. If a directive is not present, the blog uses its normal behavior. Write each directive name carefully, since a misspelled name is simply ignored.

The Video Directives

Video directives let a post play a video without the editor's video window. They cover the video type, the YouTube or Vimeo identifier, a poster image, the file locations for small, medium, and large video sources, a captions file, and the cross-origin setting. Most writers use the editor for video instead. See Video in a Post.

The Search and Social Directives

Some directives set the page's title, description, and the picture shared on social networks. These override the values the blog would otherwise build. Use them only when the automatic value is wrong for a specific post, since the editor's own fields already supply these in most cases.

The blog also reads a template directive that includes a custom template in the post.

JSON-LD

JSON-LD is structured data, a block of machine-readable information that search engines use to understand a page. Galaxie Blog generates it for each post. The Post JSON-LD window shows the block for a post, so you can see what search engines receive.

Check the output before you change anything. The generated data is correct for most posts, and a wrong edit can make a search result misleading. Make changes only when you know what the field means.

When to Use These

  • Use a social image or description directive when a post's shared preview is wrong, and the editor's fields do not fix it.
  • Use a video directive when you are embedding a video the editor does not support.
  • Leave JSON-LD alone unless you have a specific reason and you know the output you need.

Gotchas

  • Check the spelling. A misspelled directive name is ignored without an error.
  • Directives can override the editor. If a preview looks wrong after an edit, check the header field for an old directive.
  • Test the result. View the page source or the social preview after a change.

PAGES.TITLE: Releasing, Promoting, and Removing a Post
PAGES.DESCRIPTION: Making a post public, emailing subscribers, promoting a post to the top of the main page, and removing a post with a redirect.
PAGES.BODY:
Every post goes through the same three states after you write it: draft, released, and, if you ever need it, removed. Promoting is an extra option that works on a released post. This page covers each step, why it works the way it does, and what the prompts ask you.

Table of Contents

  • Drafts and Release
  • How to Release a Post
  • Releasing Versus Emailing Subscribers
  • How to Promote a Post
  • Promote vs Pin
  • How to Remove a Post
  • How to Delete a Removed Post
  • Removing vs Deleting
  • After You Remove a Post
  • Gotchas
  • See Also

Drafts and Release

A new post is saved as a draft and is not visible on the blog until you release it. That gives you time to reread the post, check the images, and fix the title before the world sees it. It also means you can save a half-finished post without it appearing on the front page by mistake.

How to Release a Post

  1. Finish the post, then check the Released box in the Misc section.
  2. Click Submit. The blog asks whether to change the Date Posted to today.
  3. Answer that question. Say yes unless you have a reason to keep an older date. See Dates and Sort Order for why the date matters.
  4. The blog then asks whether to email the post to your subscribers. Say yes to send it now, or no to send it later.

If you say no, you can email the post later: the blog asks again each time you save the released post. Once a post has been emailed, the prompt asks whether to send it again. Saying yes always sends it, so only say yes when the post has changed enough to be worth a second email. Pages are never emailed.

Saving a released post also clears its cached page, so the change shows up right away.

Releasing Versus Emailing Subscribers

Some posts are for the site, not for the inbox, such as a small fix or a correction. Asking every time lets you decide, rather than sending an email you cannot take back. For posts that should go out automatically, use Scheduling a Post, where the email goes out at the release time.

How to Promote a Post

Promoting a post moves it above the rest of the main page, no matter its date. It is useful for an announcement, a new release, or a post you want readers to see first. To promote a post, open it, check Promote in the Misc section, and click Submit.

A promoted post is marked with a loudspeaker icon and a highlight in the theme's main color, so readers can tell it is an announcement. Clear the box and submit again to return the post to its normal place in the list. Promotion works for blog posts, not pages.

Promote vs Pin

Promotion is a marker on the post, not a fixed slot on the page. Several promoted posts stay in order by their sort date, and when you stop promoting a post, it drops back into the list without you having to move anything else.

How to Remove a Post

Removing a post takes it off the public blog, but keeps it in the database, so you can bring it back. To remove a post, open it, check Remove in the Misc section, and submit. The blog asks you to confirm, because readers will no longer see the post.

If the post was released, the blog then asks whether to create a redirect. A redirect sends anyone who opens the old address to another page. Choose Permanent (301) when the content has moved for good, or Temporary (302) when it will come back. See Post URLs and Redirects.

How to Delete a Removed Post

Deleting is the permanent step. Open a removed post in the editor, and a highlighted message appears: "This post has been removed and you may permanently delete it." Click the delete link in that message to remove the post for good. Deleting also removes its redirect.

You do not have to delete. A removed post can stay in the database for later use.

Removing vs Deleting

Removing and deleting are separate on purpose. Removing is reversible and quick. Deleting is final, so the blog makes you do it on a post that is already off the site. That gives you a chance to change your mind, and to decide about the redirect first.

After You Remove a Post

Search engines keep old results for a while. If a post was indexed, it can still show up in search after you remove it. A redirect helps readers who follow old links. Google's own removal tools can speed up the removal from its results.

Gotchas

  • Answer the date prompt on purpose. A date that is too old can keep a post out of some RSS readers.
  • A removed post is hidden from readers, but administrators can still open it in the editor.
  • Deleting removes the redirect too. If you want the redirect kept, leave the post removed and do not delete it.
